whatIsIt: An array is a collection of elements stored in contiguous memory, each reachable directly by its index.
Think of it like a row of numbered mailboxes on a street — if you know the box number, you can walk straight to it without checking every box along the way.

steps.title: Contiguous Memory
steps.body: All elements sit back-to-back in one memory block, so the whole array can be described by a single starting address.

steps.title: Index-Based Addressing
steps.body: Any element's address is computed directly — no searching required: address = base + (index × elementSize).

steps.title: Fixed Capacity, Amortized Growth
steps.body: A raw array has a fixed size. Dynamic arrays (like Kotlin's ArrayList) grow by allocating a bigger backing array and copying everything over when full.

steps.title: Shifting on Insert/Delete
steps.body: Inserting or deleting anywhere but the end means shifting every following element one slot over, to keep the array contiguous.

formulas.label: Access by index
formulas.note: Direct address computation — no traversal needed.

formulas.label: Search (unsorted)
formulas.note: Worst case checks every element.

formulas.label: Insert / Delete at end
formulas.note: *Amortized — occasional O(n) resize when capacity is exceeded.

formulas.label: Insert / Delete at start or middle
formulas.note: Every following element must shift by one position.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements currently in the array
constant time — independent of n
linear time — grows proportionally with n

codeBlocks.title: Dynamic Array — core operations
Complexity summary

applications.title: Image Pixel Buffers
applications.body: Bitmaps store pixels in a flat array, indexed by row × width + column, for fast direct access.

applications.title: Spreadsheets & Tables
applications.body: Rows and columns map naturally onto 2D arrays, giving O(1) access to any cell.

applications.title: CPU Cache Friendliness
applications.body: Contiguous memory means sequential access patterns benefit heavily from CPU cache prefetching.

applications.title: Backing Store for Other Structures
applications.body: ArrayLists, stacks, heaps, and hash tables are all commonly implemented on top of a resizable array.

takeaways: Arrays give O(1) random access because element addresses are computed, not searched for.
Dynamic arrays grow by allocating a bigger array and copying — expensive per-call, but O(1) amortized over many appends.
Inserting or deleting in the middle costs O(n) because following elements must shift.
Contiguous memory layout makes arrays very CPU cache-friendly for sequential access.
Arrays are the foundation most other data structures (lists, stacks, heaps, hash tables) are built on top of.

figure.caption: Contiguity is the whole bargain. Every element is the same size and sits next to the last, so a[i] is one multiply-and-add — no search, no pointer chase. The same layout is why inserting at the front has to shift everything after it.

whatIsIt: A string is a sequence of characters stored much like an array — each character sits at a known index and is reachable directly.
In many languages strings are immutable: operations that look like edits actually build a brand-new string rather than changing the original.

steps.title: Index Access
steps.body: Read the character at any position in O(1), exactly like an array element.

steps.title: Concatenation
steps.body: Joining two strings copies both into a new buffer — cost grows with total length.

steps.title: Substring / Slice
steps.body: Extract a contiguous range of characters, typically by copying that range out.

steps.title: Immutability
steps.body: Because the buffer can't change in place, repeated edits should use a mutable builder instead.

formulas.label: Index / Length
formulas.note: Character lookup and length are direct reads.

formulas.label: Concatenation
formulas.note: Both strings are copied into the new buffer.

formulas.label: Search (naive)
formulas.note: Checking every start position for a pattern of length m.

notationKey.meaning: length of the string
length of a pattern or second string

codeBlocks.title: Building strings efficiently

applications.title: Text Search
applications.body: Find/replace, autocomplete, and log grepping all reduce to substring and pattern matching over strings.

applications.title: Parsing & Tokenizing
applications.body: Compilers, URL routers, and CSV readers slice strings into meaningful tokens.

applications.title: Serialization
applications.body: JSON, logs, and network payloads are exchanged as strings before being parsed back into data.

takeaways: A string behaves like an immutable array of characters — index access is O(1).
Repeated concatenation in a loop is O(n²); use a string builder for O(n).
Substring and concatenation copy characters, so their cost scales with length.
Most real work on strings is search and parsing, which build on array-style traversal.

figure.caption: A string is an array with text-specific operations bolted on — and in most languages an *immutable* one, so every "edit" allocates a new block. That is why building a string in a loop is quadratic unless a builder or list-join collects the pieces first.

whatIsIt: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node — there's no requirement that nodes sit next to each other in memory.
Think of it like a scavenger hunt: each clue tells you where to find the next one, but you can't jump ahead without following the chain.

steps.title: Node Structure
steps.body: Each node bundles a value with a reference to the next node — the last node's next is null.

steps.title: Head Pointer
steps.body: The list only tracks its head; every other node is reached by following next pointers from there.

steps.title: O(1) Insert at Head
steps.body: Inserting at the front just points the new node at the old head — no shifting, unlike an array.

steps.title: O(n) Access
steps.body: There's no index math — reaching the k-th node means walking k pointers from the head.

formulas.label: Insert / Delete at head
formulas.note: Just repoint the head — no shifting needed.

formulas.label: Insert / Delete at tail
formulas.note: *O(1) if a tail pointer is maintained; O(n) to find it otherwise.

formulas.label: Access / Search by value
formulas.note: Must walk from the head — no direct addressing.

notationKey.meaning: number of nodes in the list
reference to the first node, or null if empty
each node's pointer to its successor

codeBlocks.title: Singly Linked List — core operations

applications.title: Undo History
applications.body: Each edit points back to the previous state, letting you walk backward without an array.

applications.title: Music/Playlist Queues
applications.body: Songs chain to the next track — inserting or removing mid-queue is O(1) once you're there.

applications.title: Memory-Constrained Allocation
applications.body: Nodes can live anywhere in memory, so a linked list doesn't need one big contiguous block.

takeaways: A linked list trades O(1) indexed access for O(1) insert/delete at the head — the opposite trade-off from an array.
There is no formula for a node's address — every access means walking pointers from the head.
Maintaining a tail pointer turns tail-append from O(n) into O(1).
Because nodes aren't contiguous, linked lists are less CPU-cache-friendly than arrays for sequential scans.

figure.caption: No index arithmetic: reaching the k-th node means walking k links, so random access is O(n). What it buys is O(1) splicing — given the node before, inserting or deleting is two pointer writes and no shifting, which an array cannot do at any position but the end.

whatIsIt: A doubly linked list chains nodes together where each node stores a value plus two pointers: one to the next node and one to the previous node.
The extra back-pointer lets you walk the list in both directions and remove a node in O(1) once you hold it — the key advantage over a singly linked list.

steps.title: Node with Two Links
steps.body: Each node holds prev and next references alongside its value.

steps.title: Insert
steps.body: Splice a node in by rewiring four pointers: the neighbors' next/prev and the new node's own two.

steps.title: Delete in O(1)
steps.body: Given a node, connect its prev directly to its next — no scan from the head needed.

steps.title: Bidirectional Traversal
steps.body: Walk forward from head via next, or backward from tail via prev.

formulas.label: Insert / Delete at a known node
formulas.note: Only a fixed number of pointers are rewired.

formulas.label: Access / Search
formulas.note: No indexing — you follow links from an end.

formulas.label: Extra space per node
formulas.note: One additional pointer versus a singly linked list.

notationKey.meaning: the first and last nodes
a node's backward and forward pointers
number of nodes

codeBlocks.title: Node and O(1) removal

applications.title: Browser & Editor History
applications.body: Back/forward navigation walks a doubly linked list of visited states in either direction.

applications.title: LRU Cache
applications.body: An LRU cache pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list to move used entries and evict the tail in O(1).

applications.title: Playlists
applications.body: Media players jump to previous or next tracks by following the two links of the current node.

takeaways: Two pointers per node buy O(1) deletion at a known node and traversal in both directions.
The cost is one extra pointer of memory per node plus more bookkeeping on every insert/delete.
Access and search are still O(n) — links give no random indexing.
The hash-map + doubly-linked-list combo is the classic O(1) LRU cache design.

figure.caption: The second pointer is the entire structural difference. With prev, a node can unlink *itself* — B.next = D and D.prev = B, no walk to find the predecessor — which is what makes it the partner structure in an LRU cache. The cost is one more pointer per node and two more writes per edit.

whatIsIt: A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) collection — elements are added and removed from the same end, called the top.
Think of a stack of plates: you can only take from the top, and the last plate you put down is the first one you pick back up.

steps.title: Push
steps.body: Adds a new element on top of the stack.

steps.title: Pop
steps.body: Removes and returns the top element.

steps.title: Peek
steps.body: Reads the top element without removing it.

steps.title: LIFO Ordering
steps.body: The most recently pushed element is always the first one popped — no access to elements underneath.

formulas.label: Push / Pop / Peek
formulas.note: All operations touch only the top element.

formulas.label: Search
formulas.note: Finding an arbitrary element means popping down to it.

notationKey.meaning: the most recently pushed element
last-in, first-out

codeBlocks.title: Stack — array-backed

applications.title: Undo/Redo
applications.body: Each action pushes onto an undo stack; undoing pops the most recent one off.

applications.title: Function Call Stack
applications.body: Every function call pushes a stack frame; returning pops it — this is how recursion is implemented under the hood.

applications.title: Browser Back Button
applications.body: Visited pages push onto a history stack; back pops the most recent page.

takeaways: A stack only exposes its top — push, pop, and peek are all O(1).
LIFO ordering makes stacks the natural fit for anything with a 'most recent first' undo semantic.
Recursion and stacks are deeply linked: every recursive call is implicitly a stack push.
Unlike a queue, a stack cannot efficiently access or remove elements from the bottom.

figure.caption: One end, two operations. Everything a stack is good at follows from that restriction: the most recent thing is the cheapest to reach, so it models nesting — call frames, bracket matching, undo — where the last context opened is always the first that must close.

columns.label: stack (top first)
columns.note: only the top is reachable — O(1) both ways

whatIsIt: A queue is a first-in, first-out (FIFO) collection — elements are added at the back and removed from the front.
Think of a checkout line: the first person to join is the first person served.

steps.title: Enqueue
steps.body: Adds a new element at the back of the queue.

steps.title: Dequeue
steps.body: Removes and returns the element at the front.

steps.title: Peek
steps.body: Reads the front element without removing it.

steps.title: FIFO Ordering
steps.body: The element that has waited longest is always served next.

formulas.label: Enqueue / Dequeue / Peek
formulas.note: A ring buffer or linked list avoids shifting on either end.

formulas.label: Search
formulas.note: Finding an arbitrary element means scanning from the front.

notationKey.meaning: the next element to be dequeued
first-in, first-out

codeBlocks.title: Queue — deque-backed

applications.title: Task Scheduling
applications.body: Print jobs, print spoolers, and CPU task queues all process work in arrival order.

applications.title: BFS Traversal
applications.body: Breadth-first search on a graph or tree uses a queue to visit nodes level by level.

applications.title: Request Buffering
applications.body: Servers queue incoming requests so bursts of traffic get processed in order instead of dropped.

takeaways: A queue only exposes its front and back — enqueue, dequeue, and peek are all O(1) with the right backing structure.
FIFO ordering makes queues the natural fit for anything that must preserve arrival order.
Breadth-first search relies on a queue the same way depth-first search relies on a stack.
A plain array-backed queue needs care (ring buffer or deque) to avoid O(n) shifting on dequeue.

figure.caption: Two ends: add at the back, remove from the front. Implemented on an array the indices wrap around modulo the capacity, so nothing is ever shifted — the empty cells behind the front are reused, and the structure is a ring rather than a line.

whatIsIt: A deque — double-ended queue — allows insertion and removal at both the front and the back in O(1), making it a stack and a queue at the same time.

It is usually built either on a doubly linked list or on a circular array with two moving indices. The array version is the one used in practice: contiguous memory, no per-element node allocation, and wraparound instead of shifting.

steps.title: Two Ends, Four Operations
steps.body: pushFront, pushBack, popFront, popBack — each touches only one end.

steps.title: Keep Head and Tail Indices
steps.body: A circular buffer stores head and size; the tail is derived, so nothing shifts.

steps.title: Wrap With Modulo
steps.body: Moving past either end wraps around the buffer: index = (head + i) mod capacity.

steps.title: Grow by Doubling
steps.body: When full, copy into a buffer twice the size — amortized O(1) per push.

formulas.label: Index mapping
formulas.note: Logical position i to physical slot.

formulas.label: Push front
formulas.note: The +capacity keeps the result non-negative.

formulas.label: Operations
formulas.note: All four ends operations; O(n) only on a resize.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Contiguous, with slack for growth.

notationKey.meaning: physical slot of the logical first element
number of elements currently stored
length of the backing array
the tail continuing at slot 0 once it passes the array's end

codeBlocks.title: Circular-buffer deque
Sliding-window maximum — the classic use

applications.title: Undo / Redo & History
applications.body: Browsers cap history by pushing new entries at one end and dropping stale ones at the other.

applications.title: Sliding-Window Extremes
applications.body: A monotonic deque answers window maximum or minimum in O(n) total.

applications.title: Work Stealing
applications.body: Thread pools push and pop their own tasks at one end while other threads steal from the far end.

takeaways: A deque is a stack and a queue at once — all four end operations are O(1).
The circular buffer avoids shifting: only head and size change.
Remember the `+ capacity` when decrementing head, or the index goes negative.
Its killer application is the monotonic deque behind sliding-window maximum.

figure.caption: A queue that gave up on choosing an end: push and pop are both O(1) at the front and the back. That symmetry is what lets it stand in for a stack, a queue, or the monotonic window structure that answers sliding-window maximum in one pass.

whatIsIt: A hash table stores key-value pairs and finds any key in expected O(1) time by turning the key into an array index with a hash function.
Because two keys can hash to the same slot (a collision), a hash table also needs a strategy — chaining or open addressing — to keep those keys apart.

steps.title: Hash the Key
steps.body: Run the key through a hash function to get a number, then mod by the bucket count to pick a slot.

steps.title: Store in a Bucket
steps.body: Place the key-value pair in that slot's bucket.

steps.title: Resolve Collisions
steps.body: When two keys land in the same slot, chain them in a list (or probe for the next open slot).

steps.title: Resize on Load
steps.body: When the table fills past its load factor, allocate a bigger array and rehash every entry.

formulas.label: Insert / Lookup / Delete
formulas.note: A good hash spreads keys evenly across buckets.

formulas.label: Worst case
formulas.note: If every key collides into one bucket, operations degrade to a linear scan.

formulas.label: Load factor
formulas.note: Kept below a threshold (often 0.75) by resizing to hold O(1) behavior.

notationKey.meaning: number of stored entries
one slot of the backing array
load factor — entries per bucket

codeBlocks.title: Separate chaining

applications.title: Language Dictionaries/Maps
applications.body: The built-in map, dict, and object types in most languages are hash tables under the hood.

applications.title: Database Indexing & Caches
applications.body: Hash indexes and in-memory caches like memcached use hashing for near-instant key lookup.

applications.title: Deduplication
applications.body: Membership sets built on hashing test 'have I seen this before?' in O(1).

takeaways: Hashing converts a key into an array index, giving O(1) average insert, lookup, and delete.
Collisions are unavoidable; chaining or open addressing keeps colliding keys separated.
A bad hash or a full table drags performance toward O(n) — load factor and resizing matter.
Hash tables trade ordering for speed: iterate a tree if you need sorted keys, a hash table if you need fast lookup.

figure.caption: The hash turns a key into a bucket index, so lookup skips the search entirely — but two keys can land in the same bucket, and then the chain has to be walked. Average O(1) is really "O(1 + chain length)", which is why the load factor is watched and the table resized.

whatIsIt: A tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes: one root at the top, and every other node linked to exactly one parent, forming branches down to leaves.
Trees have no cycles — there is exactly one path between any two nodes — which is what separates a tree from a general graph.

steps.title: Root & Children
steps.body: Start from the root; each node points to zero or more child nodes.

steps.title: Depth & Height
steps.body: Depth counts edges from the root down; height counts edges from a node to its deepest leaf.

steps.title: Traversal
steps.body: Visit nodes in a defined order — pre/in/post-order (DFS) or level-order (BFS).

steps.title: Recursion
steps.body: Most tree operations are naturally recursive: solve for the children, then combine at the parent.

formulas.label: Traversal
formulas.note: Every node is visited exactly once.

formulas.label: Height (balanced)
formulas.note: A balanced tree of n nodes is about log n levels tall.

formulas.label: Height (degenerate)
formulas.note: A tree shaped like a chain is as tall as it is large.

notationKey.meaning: the single top node with no parent
a node with no children
total number of nodes
height — longest root-to-leaf path

codeBlocks.title: Node and recursive traversal

applications.title: File Systems
applications.body: Folders and files form a tree: each directory is a node whose children are its contents.

applications.title: DOM & UI Trees
applications.body: An HTML page is a tree of nested elements; UI frameworks render and diff that hierarchy.

applications.title: Org Charts & Taxonomies
applications.body: Any parent-child hierarchy — company reporting lines, biological classification — is a tree.

takeaways: A tree is an acyclic hierarchy: one root, one parent per node, exactly one path between any two nodes.
Traversal touches every node once (O(n)); most tree logic is naturally recursive.
A balanced tree is ~log n tall, which is what makes tree-based lookups fast.
Let a tree degenerate into a chain and its height — and its operations — slide back to O(n).

figure.caption: One parent per node and no cycles, which is the whole definition — and it forces the edge count to be exactly n − 1. Everything else is vocabulary: depth counts down from the root, height counts up from the deepest leaf, and a node's subtree is a tree in its own right.

whatIsIt: A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree where every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree holds larger values.
That ordering invariant is what turns a tree shape into a fast search structure — at each node you know which side to descend into.

steps.title: Ordering Invariant
steps.body: left.value < node.value < right.value holds at every node, recursively.

steps.title: Search
steps.body: Compare the target to the current node and descend left or right — halving the remaining space each step, if balanced.

steps.title: Insert
steps.body: Walk down as if searching for the value, then attach a new node where the search would have failed.

steps.title: Balance Matters
steps.body: An unbalanced BST (e.g. inserted in sorted order) degrades to a linked list — O(n) instead of O(log n).

formulas.label: Search / Insert / Delete (balanced)
formulas.note: Each comparison eliminates roughly half the remaining tree.

formulas.label: Search / Insert / Delete (worst case)
formulas.note: An unbalanced tree can degrade to a straight chain.

notationKey.meaning: number of nodes in the tree
height of the tree — log₂n when balanced, n when degenerate

codeBlocks.title: Binary Search Tree — search & insert

applications.title: Ordered Sets & Maps
applications.body: TreeSet/TreeMap-style structures use a balanced BST to keep keys sorted while staying O(log n).

applications.title: Database Indexes
applications.body: B-Trees (BST cousins) back most database indexes for fast range and equality lookups.

applications.title: Autocomplete Ranges
applications.body: Range queries like 'all names between M and P' fall out naturally from in-order traversal.

takeaways: A BST's speed comes from its ordering invariant, not from any special node type.
Balanced BSTs give O(log n) search/insert/delete; unbalanced ones can degrade to O(n).
Self-balancing variants (AVL, Red-Black) exist specifically to guarantee the balanced case.
In-order traversal of a BST always yields values in sorted order.

figure.caption: The invariant is about whole subtrees, not neighbours: everything left of a node is smaller, everything right is larger. That is what lets a search discard half the tree per step — O(height), which is O(log n) only while the tree stays balanced. Insert 1,2,3,4,5 in order and it degenerates into a linked list with O(n) lookups.

whatIsIt: A heap is a complete binary tree that maintains the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is ≤ its children, so the smallest element is always at the root (a max-heap keeps the largest).
Because the tree is complete, it packs perfectly into an array — a node at index i finds its children at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so no pointers are needed.

steps.title: Peek the Root
steps.body: The min (or max) is always at index 0 — reading it is O(1).

steps.title: Insert & Sift Up
steps.body: Add at the end, then swap it upward with its parent until the heap property holds.

steps.title: Extract & Sift Down
steps.body: Move the last element to the root, remove the old root, then swap it downward with its smaller child.

steps.title: Array Layout
steps.body: Parent/child links are computed from indices, so the whole structure lives in one flat array.

formulas.label: Peek min/max
formulas.note: The extreme element is always at the root.

formulas.label: Insert / Extract
formulas.note: Sift up or down travels at most the height of the tree.

formulas.label: Build heap
formulas.note: Heapifying an existing array is linear, not n log n.

notationKey.meaning: index 0 — the min (min-heap) or max (max-heap)
a node's array index; children at 2i+1 and 2i+2
number of elements

codeBlocks.title: Min-heap insert (sift up)

applications.title: Priority Queues
applications.body: A heap is the standard backing for a priority queue — always serve the highest-priority item next.

applications.title: Dijkstra & A*
applications.body: Shortest-path search pulls the closest unvisited node from a min-heap each step.

applications.title: Top-K & Streaming Medians
applications.body: A size-k heap tracks the k largest elements of a stream without sorting everything.

takeaways: A heap gives O(1) access to the min or max and O(log n) insert/extract — perfect for priority queues.
Completeness lets a heap live in a flat array with index arithmetic instead of node pointers.
Building a heap from an array is O(n); heapsort then extracts in O(n log n).
A heap orders only along root-to-leaf paths — siblings are unordered, so it isn't a sorted structure.

figure.caption: A heap is ordered only *vertically*: every parent beats its children, and siblings are unrelated. That weaker promise is why push and pop are O(log n) while the root stays correct for free — and because the tree is complete, it needs no pointers at all: child indices are 2i+1 and 2i+2 in a plain array.

whatIsIt: A trie (prefix tree) stores a set of strings as a tree of characters: each edge is one character, and each root-to-node path spells out a prefix.
Words that share a prefix share the same path, so lookups depend on the length of the word — not on how many words the trie holds.

steps.title: Character Edges
steps.body: Each node has one child per possible next character, keyed by that character.

steps.title: Insert a Word
steps.body: Walk down from the root creating nodes for each character, then mark the final node as end-of-word.

steps.title: Search / Prefix
steps.body: Follow the characters from the root; if the path exists you found the prefix — check the end flag for a full word.

steps.title: Shared Prefixes
steps.body: Common beginnings are stored once, which is what makes prefix queries fast.

formulas.label: Insert / Search
formulas.note: L is the length of the word — independent of how many keys are stored.

formulas.label: Prefix query
formulas.note: Walking to the end of the prefix takes one step per character.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Nodes hold a slot per possible next character.

notationKey.meaning: length of the query word or prefix
flag marking a node as a complete word
the set of possible characters at each node

codeBlocks.title: Trie insert and prefix check

applications.title: Autocomplete
applications.body: Type-ahead suggestions walk to the prefix node, then list every word beneath it.

applications.title: Spell Check & Dictionaries
applications.body: Membership tests and prefix validation run in time proportional to word length.

applications.title: IP Routing
applications.body: Routers use trie variants (radix trees) to match the longest network prefix for an address.

takeaways: A trie keys strings by character path, so lookup is O(L) regardless of how many words it holds.
Shared prefixes are stored once, making prefix and autocomplete queries its signature strength.
The cost is memory: each node reserves room for its possible next characters.
Use a trie for prefix-heavy work; use a hash table when you only need exact-key lookup.

figure.caption: Cost scales with the *word*, not the dictionary: "cart" is found in four steps whether the trie holds ten words or ten million. The price is space — one node per character per distinct prefix — which is why the children are usually a small map rather than a full alphabet-sized array.

whatIsIt: A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges, which may be directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted.
Think of a city's road map: intersections are vertices, roads are edges, and one-way streets are directed edges.

steps.title: Vertices & Edges
steps.body: A graph is defined by a set of vertices V and a set of edges E connecting pairs of vertices.

steps.title: Adjacency Representation
steps.body: Graphs are stored as an adjacency list (per-vertex neighbor list) or adjacency matrix (V×V grid).

steps.title: Traversal
steps.body: BFS explores level by level using a queue; DFS explores as deep as possible first using a stack or recursion.

steps.title: Weighted Paths
steps.body: When edges carry weights, shortest-path algorithms like Dijkstra's replace simple traversal.

formulas.label: BFS / DFS traversal
formulas.note: Every vertex and edge is visited once.

formulas.label: Adjacency matrix space
formulas.note: One cell per possible vertex pair, regardless of edge count.

formulas.label: Adjacency list space
formulas.note: One entry per vertex plus one per edge — better for sparse graphs.

notationKey.meaning: number of vertices
number of edges
the list of neighbors of vertex u

codeBlocks.title: Graph — adjacency list + BFS

applications.title: Navigation & Routing
applications.body: Road networks and flight routes are graphs; shortest-path algorithms power turn-by-turn directions.

applications.title: Social Networks
applications.body: People are vertices, friendships/follows are edges — traversal powers 'friends of friends' features.

applications.title: Dependency Resolution
applications.body: Package managers model dependencies as a directed graph and topologically sort it to install in order.

takeaways: A graph generalizes trees and linked lists — any node can connect to any other node, including cycles.
Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs (few edges); adjacency matrices suit dense graphs (many edges).
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS is naturally suited to cycle detection and topological sort.
Weighted shortest-path problems need Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, or Floyd-Warshall instead of plain BFS.

figure.caption: Nodes and edges, and nothing else is promised — no root, no order, cycles allowed. The representation is the real decision: an adjacency list costs O(V + E) space and lists a node's neighbours instantly, while a matrix costs O(V²) but answers "is there an edge" in O(1). Dense graphs favour the matrix; almost everything else favours the list.

whatIsIt: A segment tree stores aggregate information over array ranges in a binary tree, answering range queries and point/range updates in O(log n).
Each node covers a contiguous segment: leaves are single elements, and each internal node combines its two children — a sum, min, max, or any associative operation.

steps.title: Build the Tree
steps.body: Recursively split the array in half; each node stores the combined value of its range.

steps.title: Query a Range
steps.body: Descend from the root, combining the nodes whose ranges fully lie inside the query.

steps.title: Update a Point
steps.body: Change a leaf, then walk back up recomputing each ancestor's combined value.

steps.title: Lazy Propagation
steps.body: For range updates, defer changes with lazy tags pushed down only when a node is next visited.

formulas.label: Query / update
formulas.note: Only O(log n) nodes are touched per operation.

formulas.label: Build
formulas.note: Bottom-up over 2n−1 nodes.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: About 2n–4n array slots for the tree.

the associative merge (sum, min, max, gcd…)

applications.title: Range Statistics
applications.body: Live sums, minimums, or maximums over changing array ranges — the segment tree's core job.

applications.body: A workhorse for problems mixing frequent range queries and updates.

takeaways: A segment tree gives O(log n) range queries and updates for any associative operation.
Lazy propagation extends it to efficient range updates, not just point updates.
It's more flexible than a Fenwick tree (min/max/gcd), at higher memory and code cost.
Build is O(n); every query or update touches only O(log n) nodes.

figure.caption: Each node owns a range and stores its aggregate, so any query range decomposes into at most two nodes per level — O(log n) of them, never more. A point update walks the single path from that leaf to the root. Unlike a Fenwick tree it holds any associative operation, min and gcd included, and with lazy propagation it takes range updates too.

whatIsIt: A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree, or BIT) supports prefix-sum queries and point updates in O(log n) using a single array and clever bit manipulation.
It's a leaner alternative to a segment tree for cumulative sums: less memory, tiny code, and blazing constants — at the cost of only handling invertible operations like addition.

steps.title: Index by Low Bit
steps.body: Each position i is responsible for a range of length equal to its lowest set bit (i & −i).

steps.title: Query a Prefix
steps.body: Sum a prefix by repeatedly subtracting the low bit: i −= i & −i until zero.

steps.title: Update a Point
steps.body: Add a delta and propagate upward: i += i & −i until past the array.

steps.title: Range = Two Prefixes
steps.body: sum(l..r) = prefix(r) − prefix(l−1).

formulas.label: Query / update
formulas.note: Each jumps over O(log n) responsible ranges.

formulas.label: Low-bit trick
formulas.note: Isolates the lowest set bit — the range size.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: A single array, roughly half a segment tree's memory.

takeaways: A Fenwick tree does prefix-sum queries and point updates in O(log n).
The i & −i low-bit trick is what makes its jumps work in one array.
It uses less memory and code than a segment tree but only handles invertible ops.

figure.caption: Every index covers a block whose length is its lowest set bit: tree[4] holds four elements, tree[6] holds two, tree[8] holds all eight. whatIsIt: A disjoint set (union-find) tracks a partition of elements into non-overlapping groups, answering 'are these two in the same group?' and merging groups almost instantly.
Each group is a tree with a representative root; two optimizations — path compression and union by rank — flatten those trees so operations run in near-constant amortized time.

steps.title: Each Element Its Own Set
steps.body: Initially every element is its own root, a singleton group.

steps.title: Find the Root
steps.body: Follow parent pointers to the representative; along the way, point nodes straight at the root (path compression).

steps.title: Union Two Sets
steps.body: Merge by attaching the smaller/shorter tree under the larger root (union by rank/size).

steps.title: Same-Set Test
steps.body: Two elements share a group iff their roots are identical.

The two optimisations attack the walk itself: union by rank never hangs a taller tree under a shorter one, and path compression re-points every node it passed straight at the root — after which the amortised cost is inverse-Ackermann, effectively O(1).

whatIsIt: AVL and red-black trees are self-balancing binary search trees: they rearrange themselves during inserts and deletes so their height stays O(log n), preventing the degenerate chains a plain BST can become.
AVL trees keep stricter balance (faster lookups), while red-black trees balance more loosely (faster updates) — the tradeoff behind why each is chosen where it is.

steps.title: Insert Like a BST
steps.body: Place the new key by ordinary binary-search-tree descent.

steps.title: Detect Imbalance
steps.body: AVL checks per-node height differences; red-black checks color rules along the path.

steps.title: Rotate to Rebalance
steps.body: Single or double rotations restructure the offending subtree in O(1) each.

steps.title: Restore Invariants
steps.body: AVL keeps balance factors in {−1,0,1}; red-black repaints and rotates to satisfy its color properties.

formulas.note: Guaranteed by the height bound.

formulas.label: AVL balance factor
formulas.note: Strict height balance.

formulas.label: Red-black height

applications.body: Red-black trees back Java's TreeMap and C++'s std::map for sorted key-value storage.

takeaways: Self-balancing BSTs guarantee O(log n) by keeping height logarithmic via rotations.
AVL is more rigidly balanced (faster search); red-black rotates less (faster insert/delete).
Both keep sorted order, unlike a hash table — enabling range and successor queries.
Red-black trees are the common choice inside standard-library ordered maps and sets.

figure.caption: Both trees buy the same thing — a height bound that survives adversarial input — and pay differently. AVL keeps heights within 1 and stays shorter (≈1.44 log n), so lookups win; red-black tolerates a longer path (≤2 log n) and rebalances less, so writes win. Inserting 1, 2, 3 into an unbalanced BST gives a chain; a single rotation makes it this.

whatIsIt: A B-tree is a balanced multi-way search tree where each node holds many keys and has many children, keeping the tree short and wide to minimize slow disk reads.
Its B+ variant stores all data in the leaves and links them in a list, making it the backbone of databases and filesystems where each node maps to a disk block.

steps.title: Many Keys per Node
steps.body: A node of order m holds up to m−1 sorted keys and up to m child pointers.

steps.title: Search by Range
steps.body: Within a node, binary-search the keys to pick which child subtree to descend into.

steps.title: Split on Overflow
steps.body: Inserting into a full node splits it, pushing the median key up to the parent.

steps.title: Merge on Underflow
steps.body: Deletion borrows from a sibling or merges nodes to keep each at least half full.

formulas.label: Height
formulas.note: High branching factor m makes the tree very shallow.

formulas.label: Search / insert / delete
formulas.note: With few node accesses — the disk-cost that matters.

formulas.label: Fill invariant
formulas.note: Every non-root node stays at least half full.

takeaways: B-trees stay short and wide, minimizing the disk/page accesses that dominate cost.

Splits and merges keep every node at least half full, bounding the height.
B+ trees, with data in linked leaves, power database indexes and filesystems.

figure.caption: Built for storage that reads in *pages*, not words: one node holds many keys, so a million records sit three or four levels deep instead of twenty. Each level costs one disk read, and that count — not the comparison count — is what the design minimises. B+ trees go further and keep all values in the leaves, chained for range scans.

whatIsIt: A suffix tree is a compressed trie of every suffix of a string, enabling substring search and many string queries in time proportional to the pattern, not the text.
A suffix array is its space-lean cousin — a sorted list of suffix start positions — that trades a little query speed for far less memory, which is why it's used more in practice.

steps.title: Enumerate Suffixes
steps.body: Consider every suffix of the text (n of them for length n).

steps.title: Build the Structure
steps.body: A suffix tree merges shared prefixes into edges; a suffix array sorts the suffixes lexicographically.

steps.title: Search a Pattern
steps.body: Walk the tree by the pattern's characters, or binary-search the sorted suffix array.

steps.title: Answer Rich Queries
steps.body: Longest repeated substring, longest common substring, and counts fall out of the structure.

formulas.label: Tree build
formulas.note: Ukkonen's algorithm builds it in linear time.

formulas.label: Pattern search
formulas.note: m is the pattern length — independent of text size.

formulas.label: Array search
formulas.note: Binary search over sorted suffixes; O(n) space.

codeBlocks.title: Suffix array — simple construction
codeBlocks.code:
// O(n^2 log n) reference build — real code uses O(n log n) or O(n).
fun suffixArray(s: String): IntArray =
    (s.indices)
        .sortedBy { s.substring(it) }   // sort suffixes lexicographically
        .toIntArray()

The companion LCP array records how much each neighbouring pair shares, which is what turns the array back into the suffix tree's answers: longest repeated substring is simply its maximum.

whatIsIt: A skip list is a sorted linked list with extra 'express lane' layers that let searches skip over many nodes, giving O(log n) expected search, insert, and delete.
Each node is randomly promoted to higher levels, so the structure balances itself probabilistically — no rotations, far simpler than a balanced tree.

steps.title: Layered Lists
steps.body: The bottom layer holds all nodes in order; each higher layer is a sparse express lane over the one below.

steps.title: Search Top-Down
steps.body: Start at the top-left, move right while the next key is ≤ target, then drop down a level.

steps.title: Randomized Height
steps.body: On insert, flip coins to decide how many levels the new node rises to.

steps.title: Splice In/Out
steps.body: Insert and delete just relink pointers at each affected level — no rebalancing.

formulas.note: Express lanes halve the search span per level.

Its simplicity and concurrency-friendliness make it popular in real systems like Redis.

figure.caption: A sorted linked list with express lanes: each node is promoted to the next level with probability ½, so the top lane skips about half the nodes, the one below a quarter, and a search drops down whenever the next hop overshoots. Expected O(log n) with no rotations and no rebalancing — the balance is probabilistic rather than maintained.

whatIsIt: A sparse table precomputes the answer for every interval whose length is a power of two, so a range query is resolved by combining just two of them.

It only works for idempotent operations — min, max, gcd, bitwise and/or — because the two intervals overlap and the overlap must not be double-counted. In exchange it beats a segment tree on queries: O(1) instead of O(log n), at the cost of being read-only.

steps.title: Level 0 Is the Array
steps.body: table[0][i] = a[i] — every interval of length 1.

steps.title: Double Each Level
steps.body: table[k][i] combines two length-2^(k−1) blocks starting at i and i + 2^(k−1).

steps.title: Pick the Largest Fitting Power
steps.body: For query [l, r], let k = ⌊log₂(r − l + 1)⌋.

steps.title: Cover the Range With Two Blocks
steps.body: Combine table[k][l] and table[k][r − 2^k + 1]; they overlap, which idempotence makes harmless.

formulas.label: Build
formulas.note: Each level is built from the one below.

formulas.label: Query
formulas.note: Two lookups, constant time.

formulas.label: Build cost
formulas.formula: O(n log n) time and space
formulas.note: log n levels of n entries.

formulas.label: Requirement
formulas.formula: op must be idempotent: op(x, x) = x
formulas.note: Sums do not qualify — use a prefix sum or segment tree instead.

notationKey.meaning: answer for a[i .. i + 2^k − 1]
level index — the log of the block length
combining a value with itself changes nothing
inclusive query range

takeaways: Two overlapping power-of-two blocks cover any range — that is why queries are O(1).
Idempotence is mandatory; overlapping blocks would double-count a sum.
The structure is read-only: any update means a full O(n log n) rebuild.
Choose a segment tree when updates are needed, a sparse table when they are not.

figure.caption: Precompute the answer for every power-of-two window, then any range is covered by two of them — overlapping in the middle, which is fine because min and max do not care about double counting. O(n log n) to build, O(1) per query, and nothing can ever be updated: the overlap trick is exactly what a sum could not use.

whatIsIt: A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic set that tests membership with one guarantee: 'definitely not present' is always correct, but 'possibly present' may be a false positive.
It stores no elements — just a bit array flipped by several hash functions — so it uses a tiny fraction of the memory a real set would, at the cost of a tunable error rate and no deletions.

steps.title: One Bit Array
steps.body: Start with m bits all zero and k independent hash functions.

steps.title: Insert
steps.body: Hash the item k ways and set all k resulting bit positions to 1.

steps.title: Query
steps.body: Hash the item the same k ways; if any of those bits is 0, it's definitely absent.

steps.title: Accept False Positives
steps.body: If all k bits are 1, it's probably present — collisions can lie, but never in the negative direction.

formulas.label: False-positive rate
formulas.note: Grows as the filter fills.

formulas.label: Optimal hashes
formulas.note: Minimizes the error for given size.

formulas.label: No false negatives
formulas.note: And elements can't be removed from a plain filter.

takeaways: A Bloom filter answers membership in tiny space, with false positives but never false negatives.
Tuning m and k trades memory against the false-positive rate.

figure.caption: k hashes set k bits per insert, and a query reports "present" only if all k are already set. whatIsIt: An LRU (least-recently-used) cache holds a fixed number of entries and, when full, evicts the one that hasn't been touched for the longest time.
The classic design pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list, giving O(1) get and put: the map finds a node instantly, the list tracks recency order.

steps.title: Get Promotes
steps.body: On a hit, move that node to the front (most recent) and return its value.

steps.title: Put Inserts
steps.body: Add or update at the front; the map now points at the new node.

steps.title: Evict the Tail
steps.body: If over capacity, remove the list's tail node and its map entry — the least recently used.

whatIsIt: Space-partitioning trees — k-d trees, quad trees, and octrees — recursively split multi-dimensional space so nearest-neighbor and range queries skip most of the data.

steps.title: Prune the Search

whatIsIt: Graphs come in many flavors — directed vs undirected, weighted vs unweighted, and multigraphs that allow parallel edges — and the variant dictates which algorithms and representations apply.

steps.title: Multiplicity

steps.title: Representation
steps.body: Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs; adjacency matrices suit dense ones or O(1) edge tests.

applications.body: Coding to the List interface lets you swap implementations without touching callers.
