applications.body: Any ordered, index-addressable sequence — history, playlists, queues of work — is a List.

takeaways: A List ADT specifies ordered, positional operations, not how they're stored.
Array backing favors indexing; linked backing favors end/splice edits.
Programming to the ADT lets the implementation change underneath.
Match the backing structure to your dominant access pattern.

figure.caption: The List *interface* — ordered, indexable, duplicates allowed — says nothing about cost. Two implementations answer the same calls with opposite performance, so the question "which list" is really "which operation runs in the loop".

whatIsIt: A Set is an abstract data type holding a collection of unique elements with no duplicates, defined by membership and the classic set operations.
Its two common implementations differ in ordering: a hash set gives O(1) average membership but no order, while a tree set keeps elements sorted at O(log n).

steps.title: Uniqueness
steps.body: Adding an element already present is a no-op — a set never holds duplicates.

steps.title: Membership Test
steps.body: The core query is 'is x in the set?', ideally in O(1) or O(log n).

steps.title: Set Algebra
steps.body: Union, intersection, and difference combine two sets element-wise.

steps.title: Ordered or Not
steps.body: Hash sets are unordered; tree sets maintain sorted iteration and range queries.

formulas.label: Hash set ops
formulas.note: add / remove / contains via hashing.

formulas.label: Tree set ops
formulas.note: Sorted order and range queries.

formulas.label: Union / intersection
formulas.note: Linear in the combined size.

notationKey.meaning: the x ∈ S test
union, intersection, difference
unordered O(1) vs ordered O(log n)

codeBlocks.title: Set operations

applications.title: Deduplication
applications.body: Collecting unique visitors, tags, or IDs is a set insertion per element.

applications.title: Fast Membership
applications.body: 'Have I seen this?' checks — visited nodes, seen tokens — use a hash set.

applications.title: Set Algebra in Queries
applications.body: Filtering by union/intersection of tag sets powers search and permission systems.

takeaways: A Set ADT stores unique elements and centers on fast membership.
Hash sets give O(1) average ops but no order; tree sets give O(log n) with sorted order.
Union, intersection, and difference express set algebra directly.
Choose a tree set only when you need ordering or range queries; otherwise a hash set.

figure.caption: A Set promises membership and no duplicates — nothing about order. Backing it with a hash table gives O(1) membership and no order at all; backing it with a balanced tree costs O(log n) and hands back sorted iteration and range queries, which the hash version cannot do.

whatIsIt: A Map (dictionary, associative array) is an abstract data type storing key-value pairs, letting you look up, insert, or remove a value by its unique key.
Like Set, it comes in a hash-backed flavor (O(1) average, unordered) and a tree-backed flavor (O(log n), keys kept sorted).

steps.title: Unique Keys
steps.body: Each key maps to exactly one value; inserting an existing key overwrites it.

steps.title: Lookup by Key
steps.body: get(key) returns its value (or absent) — the map's defining operation.

steps.title: Insert & Delete
steps.body: put(key, value) and remove(key) maintain the association.

steps.title: Ordered or Not
steps.body: Hash maps iterate in no fixed order; tree maps iterate keys in sorted order.

formulas.label: Hash map ops
formulas.note: get / put / remove via hashing.

formulas.label: Tree map ops
formulas.note: Sorted keys, range and successor queries.

formulas.label: Worst case (hash)
formulas.note: Pathological collisions degrade to a scan.

notationKey.meaning: the stored association
core map operations
unordered O(1) vs ordered O(log n)

codeBlocks.title: The Map contract
codeBlocks.code:
interface Map<K, V> {
    fun get(key: K): V?          // value or null if absent
    fun put(key: K, value: V)    // insert or overwrite
    fun remove(key: K): V?
    fun containsKey(key: K): Boolean
    val size: Int
}

applications.title: Everywhere in Code
applications.body: Config lookups, caches, counters, and indexes are all maps under the hood.

applications.title: Frequency & Grouping
applications.body: Counting occurrences and grouping records by key are one-line map operations.

applications.title: Sorted Directories
applications.body: Tree maps back ordered indexes where you iterate or range-scan by key.

takeaways: A Map ADT associates unique keys with values and centers on lookup by key.
Hash maps give O(1) average access unordered; tree maps give O(log n) with sorted keys.
It's the most-used data structure in practice — the default for lookups and counting.
A Set is just a Map without values; a Map is a Set of keys carrying payloads.

figure.caption: Same trade one level up: a Map is key → value with unique keys, and the backing structure decides what else you get. Hash for speed, tree for order, insertion-ordered hash when iteration has to be predictable — the interface is identical in all three.

whatIsIt: A Priority Queue is an abstract data type that always serves the highest- (or lowest-) priority element next, regardless of insertion order.
It's almost always implemented with a binary heap, giving O(log n) insert and remove and O(1) peek at the top-priority element.

steps.title: Priority, Not Arrival
steps.body: Unlike a FIFO queue, order of service is by priority value.

steps.title: Peek the Top
steps.body: The min (or max) priority element is always available in O(1).

steps.title: Insert (Enqueue)
steps.body: Add an element; the heap sifts it into place in O(log n).

steps.title: Extract (Dequeue)
steps.body: Remove the top-priority element; the heap re-heapifies in O(log n).

formulas.label: Peek
formulas.note: The extreme element sits at the heap root.

formulas.label: Insert / Extract
formulas.note: Sift up or down the height of the heap.

formulas.label: Build from n items
formulas.note: Bottom-up heapify beats n inserts.

notationKey.meaning: the key deciding service order
read vs remove the top element
the usual backing structure

codeBlocks.title: Priority queue via a heap
codeBlocks.code:
// Min-priority queue: smallest value served first.
val pq = java.util.PriorityQueue<Int>()
pq.add(5); pq.add(1); pq.add(3)

val top = pq.peek()     // 1  — O(1)
val next = pq.poll()    // 1  — O(log n), removes it

// Max-priority: supply a reverse comparator.
val maxPq = java.util.PriorityQueue<Int>(compareByDescending { it })

applications.title: Shortest-Path Search
applications.body: Dijkstra's and A* pull the closest frontier node from a priority queue each step.

applications.title: Schedulers
applications.body: OS task schedulers and event simulations dequeue the next job by priority or timestamp.

applications.title: Streaming Top-K & Merging
applications.body: Merging k sorted streams and tracking top-K elements both lean on a priority queue.

takeaways: A Priority Queue serves elements by priority, not arrival order.
A binary heap gives O(log n) insert/extract and O(1) peek — the standard implementation.
It's the engine behind Dijkstra's, A*, Huffman coding, and event scheduling.
For strict FIFO, use a plain queue; the priority queue reorders by key.

figure.caption: "Give me the smallest" is the only promise, and the heap is the implementation that balances it: nothing is fully sorted, just enough order is kept for the root to be correct. The two array versions each make one operation free by making the other linear.

whatIsIt: Bubble sort repeatedly steps through an array, swapping adjacent elements that are out of order, until no swaps are needed.
The name comes from how larger elements 'bubble up' toward the end of the array with each pass.

steps.title: Compare Neighbors
steps.body: Walk the array comparing each adjacent pair of elements.

steps.title: Swap if Out of Order
steps.body: If the left element is greater than the right, swap them.

steps.title: Repeat Passes
steps.body: After each full pass, the largest unsorted element has bubbled to its correct position.

steps.title: Early Exit
steps.body: If a pass makes no swaps, the array is already sorted — stop early.

formulas.label: Time complexity (average/worst)
formulas.note: Nested passes over the array — quadratic comparisons.

formulas.label: Time complexity (best, sorted input)
formulas.note: With the early-exit optimization, one pass confirms it's sorted.

formulas.label: Space complexity
formulas.note: Sorts in place — no auxiliary array needed.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements in the array
flag tracking whether any swap happened in a pass

codeBlocks.title: Bubble Sort — with early exit

applications.title: Teaching Sorting Concepts
applications.body: Its simplicity makes bubble sort the standard first example for comparison-based sorting.

applications.title: Nearly-Sorted Data
applications.body: With the early-exit check, bubble sort runs in near-linear time on data that's already almost sorted.

takeaways: Bubble sort is O(n²) in the general case — rarely used in production for large datasets.
It sorts in place with O(1) extra space, unlike merge sort's O(n).
The early-exit optimization makes it O(n) best-case on already-sorted input.
Its main value today is pedagogical — it's the clearest introduction to comparison-and-swap sorting.

figure.caption: Only adjacent pairs are ever compared, so each pass drags the largest remaining value to the end and the sorted tail grows by exactly one. The one thing it has over the other quadratic sorts: a pass with no swap proves the array is sorted, making the best case O(n).

whatIsIt: Selection sort builds the sorted array one slot at a time by repeatedly finding the smallest remaining element and swapping it into place.
It splits the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted suffix, growing the prefix by one element on every pass.

steps.title: Scan for the Minimum
steps.body: Search the unsorted suffix for the smallest element.

steps.title: Swap Into Place
steps.body: Swap that minimum with the first unsorted position.

steps.title: Grow the Sorted Prefix
steps.body: The boundary between sorted and unsorted moves one step right.

steps.title: Repeat n Times
steps.body: Each pass locks in one more element until the whole array is sorted.

formulas.label: Time (all cases)
formulas.note: Every pass scans the rest of the array, regardless of input order.

formulas.label: Swaps
formulas.note: At most one swap per pass — the fewest of the simple sorts.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Sorts in place with a constant number of variables.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements
boundary between the sorted prefix and unsorted suffix
index of the smallest remaining element

codeBlocks.title: Selection sort

applications.title: Minimizing Writes
applications.body: When a swap is far more expensive than a comparison (e.g. flash memory), selection sort's ≤ n swaps win.

applications.title: Teaching Baseline
applications.body: Its simple 'find the smallest, put it first' loop makes it a classic first sorting algorithm.

applications.title: Partial Sort / Top-K
applications.body: Running only k passes yields the k smallest elements without sorting the rest.

takeaways: Selection sort is always O(n²) — it scans the whole remaining array even if the input is already sorted.
It makes the fewest swaps of the simple sorts (≤ n), useful when writes are costly.
It is not stable by default and gains nothing from nearly-sorted input.
Prefer insertion sort for nearly-sorted data and a divide-and-conquer sort for large arrays.

figure.caption: Scan the unsorted region for its minimum, then put it in place — always n−1 swaps, no matter what order the input arrived in. That is the only reason to reach for it: when a write is far more expensive than a comparison, nothing else moves data less.

whatIsIt: Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix one element at a time, taking the next element and sliding it left until it sits in the right spot.
It works the way most people sort a hand of playing cards: pick up the next card and insert it into its correct position among the cards already held.

steps.title: Take the Next Element
steps.body: Treat the first element as a sorted prefix; pick up the next unsorted one.

steps.title: Shift Larger Elements Right
steps.body: Compare leftward, shifting bigger elements one slot to the right to open a gap.

steps.title: Drop Into the Gap
steps.body: Place the picked element where the shifting stopped.

steps.title: Extend the Sorted Prefix
steps.body: Repeat until every element has been inserted.

formulas.label: Best case (sorted)
formulas.note: Each element only compares once and stays put.

formulas.label: Average / worst
formulas.note: Reversed input shifts every element past all its predecessors.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: In-place, and stable — equal elements keep their order.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements
the element currently being inserted
scan index moving left through the sorted prefix

codeBlocks.title: Insertion sort

applications.title: Nearly-Sorted Data
applications.body: On almost-sorted input it runs in near-linear time, ideal for keeping a live list ordered as items trickle in.

applications.title: Small Subarrays
applications.body: Fast sorts like quicksort switch to insertion sort for tiny partitions where its low overhead wins.

applications.title: Online Sorting
applications.body: It can sort a stream as elements arrive, inserting each new value into the already-sorted portion.

takeaways: Insertion sort is O(n²) in general but O(n) on nearly-sorted input — a real strength.
It is in-place, stable, and simple, making it the go-to for small or almost-sorted arrays.
Production sorts use it as the base case for their smallest partitions.
For large, randomly-ordered data, a divide-and-conquer sort is far faster.

figure.caption: The prefix is always sorted; each new element slides left until it lands. Work is proportional to how far elements have to move, so a nearly-sorted array costs O(n) — which is why real sorts (Timsort, introsort) switch to it once the subarrays get small.

whatIsIt: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer sort that splits an array in half, recursively sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves back together.
The merge step is the key insight: merging two already-sorted lists into one sorted list only takes a single linear pass.

steps.title: Divide
steps.body: Split the array into two halves, recursively, until each piece has one element.

steps.title: Conquer
steps.body: A single-element array is trivially sorted — that's the base case.

steps.title: Merge
steps.body: Combine two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front element from either side.

steps.title: Stable & Predictable
steps.body: Merge sort's runtime is O(n log n) in every case — best, average, and worst.

formulas.label: Time complexity (all cases)
formulas.note: log n levels of splitting, O(n) merge work at each level.

formulas.label: Space complexity
formulas.note: Merging needs an auxiliary array the size of the input.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements in the array
the split point of the current subarray

codeBlocks.title: Merge Sort

applications.title: External Sorting
applications.body: Sorting data too large for memory reads/merges chunks from disk — the same merge step scales up.

applications.title: Stable Sort Requirements
applications.body: Merge sort preserves the relative order of equal elements, which matters for multi-key sorts.

applications.title: Guaranteed Worst-Case Bound
applications.body: Systems needing predictable O(n log n) even on adversarial input prefer merge sort over quicksort.

takeaways: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) in every case — no worst-case O(n²) like quicksort's pivot-unlucky scenario.
The trade-off is O(n) extra space for the merge step, unlike in-place quicksort.
Merge sort is stable — equal elements keep their original relative order.
The divide-and-conquer pattern here (split, recurse, combine) reappears throughout algorithm design.

figure.caption: The merge is where the work happens: two already-sorted halves are walked in step, and taking the smaller head each time costs one comparison per output element. Equal values take from the left half first — that tie-break is the whole of stability — and the output needs its own array, which is the O(n) space quicksort does not pay.

shape.auxLabel: remaining heads — left half 4, 8 · right half 5, 9

whatIsIt: Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer sort that picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, then recursively sorts each side.
The partition step does all the work — once the pivot is in its final position, the two sides can be sorted independently.

steps.title: Choose a Pivot
steps.body: Pick an element (first, last, random, or median-of-three) to partition around.

steps.title: Partition
steps.body: Rearrange so everything smaller than the pivot is left of it and everything larger is right.

steps.title: Pivot Is Final
steps.body: After partitioning the pivot sits in its correct sorted position and never moves again.

steps.title: Recurse Both Sides
steps.body: Apply the same process to the left and right subarrays until they're size ≤ 1.

formulas.label: Average / best
formulas.note: Balanced partitions halve the array log n times.

formulas.label: Worst case
formulas.note: Consistently bad pivots (e.g. already-sorted input, first-element pivot) shrink by one.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: In-place, but recursion uses stack proportional to depth.

notationKey.meaning: the element partitioned around
current subarray boundaries
the pivot's final index after partitioning

codeBlocks.title: Quick sort (Lomuto partition)

applications.title: Standard Library Sorts
applications.body: Many language runtimes use quicksort variants (introsort) as their default in-memory sort.

applications.title: Quickselect
applications.body: The same partition step finds the k-th smallest element in expected linear time without full sorting.

applications.title: Cache-Friendly Sorting
applications.body: Its in-place, sequential access pattern makes it fast on real hardware despite the worst case.

takeaways: Quick sort averages O(n log n) and sorts in place, making it the default for many libraries.
Its Achilles' heel is O(n²) on bad pivots; randomized or median-of-three pivots avoid it in practice.
The partition routine is reusable — quickselect finds order statistics with it.
Unlike merge sort it is not stable, so use merge sort when equal-key order must be preserved.

figure.caption: Partition puts the pivot at its final index and needs no extra array — that in-place property is why it beats merge sort in practice despite the same average bound. The cost is the worst case: a first-element pivot on already-sorted input splits 0 and n−1 every time, which is O(n²). A random or median-of-three pivot is what removes it.

whatIsIt: Heap sort turns the array into a max-heap, then repeatedly extracts the largest element to the end, shrinking the heap until the array is sorted.
It combines the O(1) max access of a heap with in-place array storage — no extra memory and a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case.

steps.title: Build a Max-Heap
steps.body: Heapify the array in place so the largest element sits at the root (index 0).

steps.title: Swap Max to the End
steps.body: Swap the root with the last heap element — the max is now in its final sorted spot.

steps.title: Shrink & Sift Down
steps.body: Reduce the heap size by one and sift the new root down to restore the heap property.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.body: Keep extracting the max until the heap holds one element and the array is sorted.

formulas.label: Time (all cases)
formulas.note: n extractions, each an O(log n) sift-down.

formulas.label: Build heap
formulas.note: Bottom-up heapify is linear, not n log n.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Sorts fully in place — no auxiliary array.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements
node index; children at 2i+1 and 2i+2
moving a node down to restore the heap property

codeBlocks.title: Heap sort

applications.title: Guaranteed Worst Case
applications.body: When O(n log n) must hold even on adversarial input, heap sort avoids quicksort's O(n²) risk.

applications.title: Memory-Constrained Systems
applications.body: Its O(1) extra space suits embedded and kernel code that can't allocate a merge buffer.

applications.title: Introsort Fallback
applications.body: Hybrid sorts start with quicksort and switch to heap sort when recursion goes too deep.

takeaways: Heap sort is O(n log n) in every case and sorts in place with O(1) extra memory.
It relies on the heap property: repeatedly extract the max and shrink the heap.
It is not stable and has poor cache locality, so quicksort often beats it in wall-clock time.
Its predictable worst case makes it the safety net inside hybrid sorts like introsort.

figure.caption: Two regions in one array: a max-heap on the left, the finished tail on the right. Each step swaps the root — the largest remaining — into the tail and sifts the new root down. O(n log n) guaranteed with O(1) extra space, but its cache behaviour and lack of stability are why quicksort usually wins in practice.

whatIsIt: Counting sort orders integers without comparing them: it counts how many times each key appears, then uses those counts to place every element directly into its final position.
It beats the O(n log n) comparison-sort barrier by exploiting a small, known range of keys — but only when that range k is not much larger than n.

steps.title: Count Occurrences
steps.body: Tally how many times each key value appears in a count array of size k.

steps.title: Prefix-Sum the Counts
steps.body: Accumulate the counts so each entry becomes the ending index for that key.

steps.title: Place Into Output
steps.body: Walk the input (right to left for stability) and drop each element at its computed index.

steps.title: Copy Back
steps.body: The output array is now sorted; copy it over the input if needed.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: One pass to count, one to place; k is the size of the key range.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: A count array of size k plus an output array of size n.

formulas.label: Best when
formulas.note: Degrades badly once the key range dwarfs the element count.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements
size of the key range (max − min + 1)
tally of occurrences per key, later prefix-summed

codeBlocks.title: Counting sort (non-negative keys)

applications.title: Sorting Small-Range Keys
applications.body: Ages, exam scores, or byte values — anything with a bounded integer range sorts in linear time.

applications.title: Radix Sort Subroutine
applications.body: Radix sort runs counting sort on each digit, relying on its stability.

applications.title: Histograms & Tallies
applications.body: The count step alone answers frequency questions used in analytics and image processing.

takeaways: Counting sort runs in O(n + k) by counting keys instead of comparing them.
It only pays off when the key range k is comparable to n — huge ranges waste memory.
Processing input right-to-left keeps it stable, which is why radix sort depends on it.
It works on integers (or things mappable to a small integer key), not arbitrary comparables.

figure.caption: No comparisons at all: count how many of each value there are, prefix-sum the counts to get final positions, then place each element. O(n + k) — linear in the input *and* the value range, so it wins only while k stays small. Walking the input backwards is what keeps it stable, which is what radix sort then depends on.

shape.auxLabel: prefix-summed counts — where each value's block ends

whatIsIt: Radix sort orders numbers by processing them one digit at a time, using a stable sort (usually counting sort) on each digit from least significant to most significant.
Because each digit-pass is stable, sorting the last digit and working up to the first leaves the whole array correctly ordered — no comparisons between full values.

steps.title: Start at the Least Significant Digit
steps.body: Sort all numbers by their ones digit first.

steps.title: Stable-Sort Each Digit
steps.body: Use counting sort so equal digits keep the order fixed by earlier passes.

steps.title: Move to the Next Digit
steps.body: Repeat for tens, hundreds, and so on toward the most significant digit.

steps.title: Fully Sorted
steps.body: After the last (highest) digit pass, the array is sorted end to end.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: d digit-passes, each a counting sort over base b.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Counting-sort buffers reused per pass.

formulas.label: Effective when
formulas.note: Linear if the number of digits d is roughly constant.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements
number of digits in the largest value
base / radix (10 for decimal, 256 for bytes)

codeBlocks.title: LSD radix sort (base 10)

applications.title: Fixed-Width Keys
applications.body: Integers, fixed-length IDs, and dates sort in linear time when their digit count is bounded.

applications.title: String Sorting
applications.body: MSD radix sort orders strings and is used in suffix-array construction.

applications.title: Large Numeric Datasets
applications.body: It outpaces comparison sorts on huge arrays of same-width numbers with a small radix.

takeaways: Radix sort avoids comparisons, sorting digit by digit in O(d · (n + b)).
It leans entirely on a stable per-digit sort — counting sort is the usual choice.
It is linear only when the digit count d stays small relative to n.
It applies to fixed-width keys (integers, strings), not arbitrary comparable objects.

figure.caption: One stable pass per digit, least significant first. Each pass only orders by that digit, and stability is what preserves the previous passes' work — swap in an unstable inner sort and the whole thing collapses. d passes over n items, so O(d · n) with no comparison between whole keys ever made.

whatIsIt: Bucket sort scatters values into a set of ordered buckets by range, sorts each bucket with a simple algorithm, then concatenates the buckets in order.

It is not a comparison sort at the top level, so it escapes the O(n log n) bound — but only when the input is spread evenly. If every value lands in one bucket the algorithm degenerates to whatever sorts that bucket, typically O(n²).

steps.title: Choose the Buckets
steps.body: Split the value range into k intervals, usually k = n so each holds about one element.

steps.title: Scatter
steps.body: Send each value to bucket ⌊k·(v − min) / (max − min + 1)⌋ in one linear pass.

steps.title: Sort Each Bucket
steps.body: Insertion sort is the usual choice — buckets are tiny and nearly sorted.

steps.title: Concatenate
steps.body: Because the buckets are already in value order, appending them yields the sorted array.

formulas.label: Bucket index
formulas.note: Linear mapping from value to bucket.

formulas.label: Average time
formulas.note: Uniform input, O(1) elements per bucket.

formulas.label: Worst time
formulas.note: All values in one bucket, sorted by insertion sort.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: The buckets themselves.

notationKey.meaning: number of buckets
extremes of the input, needed to scale the mapping
equal elements keep their order if the per-bucket sort is stable

codeBlocks.title: Bucket sort with insertion sort per bucket

applications.title: Histogram & Percentile Work
applications.body: Data already binned for a histogram is one scatter pass away from being sorted.

applications.title: External & Parallel Sorting
applications.body: Buckets map cleanly onto files or worker threads, each sorted independently.

applications.title: Uniform Float Keys
applications.body: Normalized scores and random keys in [0, 1) are the textbook happy case.

takeaways: Bucket sort is linear only when the input spreads evenly across buckets.
Skewed data collapses it into the per-bucket sort's complexity — usually quadratic.
It needs to know the value range, unlike a comparison sort.
Radix sort is the related idea applied digit by digit, with a guaranteed bound.

figure.caption: Scatter into buckets by value range, sort each one, concatenate. It is O(n) *only* while the input is spread evenly — the assumption is doing all the work. Skewed data piles into one bucket and the cost collapses back to whatever sort runs inside it.

whatIsIt: Linear search looks for a target by checking each element in order until it finds a match or reaches the end.
It makes no assumptions about the data — the array need not be sorted — which is why it is the fallback whenever no structure can be exploited.

steps.title: Start at the Beginning
steps.body: Point at the first element of the collection.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Check whether the current element equals the target.

steps.title: Advance or Stop
steps.body: On a match, return the index; otherwise move to the next element.

steps.title: Exhaust the List
steps.body: If the end is reached without a match, the target isn't present.

formulas.label: Worst / average
formulas.note: May have to inspect every element.

formulas.label: Best case
formulas.note: The target is the first element checked.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Only a running index is needed.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements
the value being searched for
current scan index

codeBlocks.title: Linear search

applications.title: Unsorted Data
applications.body: When data has no order or index, scanning every element is the only correct option.

applications.title: Small Collections
applications.body: For a handful of elements its zero setup cost beats building a hash table or sorting first.

applications.title: Finding All Matches
applications.body: It naturally collects every element satisfying a predicate in one pass, not just the first.

takeaways: Linear search is O(n) but needs no sorted or indexed data — the universal fallback.
It is the right tool for small or one-off searches where preprocessing isn't worth it.
For repeated lookups on large data, sort and binary-search or build a hash table instead.
It generalizes to any sequence and any match condition, not just equality on arrays.

figure.caption: The only search with no precondition — no sorting, no index, no random access — which is why it is the one that works on a linked list or a stream. Every miss costs the full n, and that is also the honest baseline the other searches are measured against.

whatIsIt: Binary search finds a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search range.
Think of looking up a word in a paper dictionary: you open to the middle, decide which half your word is in, and repeat — never scanning page by page.

steps.title: Requires Sorted Input
steps.body: Binary search only works because the array is sorted — that's what lets you discard half each step.

steps.title: Check the Middle
steps.body: Compare the target to the middle element of the current range.

steps.title: Discard Half
steps.body: If the target is smaller, discard the right half; if larger, discard the left half.

steps.title: Repeat Until Found
steps.body: Keep halving the range until the target is found or the range is empty.

formulas.label: Time complexity
formulas.note: Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements.

formulas.label: Space complexity
formulas.note: Iterative version needs only a few index variables.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements in the array
current search range boundaries
the midpoint index being checked

codeBlocks.title: Binary Search — iterative

applications.title: Dictionary/Index Lookups
applications.body: Any sorted lookup table — word lists, sorted database indexes — searches in logarithmic time.

applications.title: Version Bisection
applications.body: `git bisect` binary-searches commit history to find the commit that introduced a bug.

applications.title: Finding Insertion Points
applications.body: Binary search variants locate where a value should be inserted to keep an array sorted.

takeaways: Binary search needs sorted input — running it on unsorted data gives wrong answers, not just slow ones.
Each comparison halves the search space, giving O(log n) time from O(n) linear search.
The classic bug is mid computation overflow; `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` avoids it.
Binary search generalizes beyond arrays to any monotonic predicate — 'find the boundary where a condition flips.'

figure.caption: Sorted input turns one comparison into a decision about half the array. The loop is three lines and still the most-failed whiteboard exercise: mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2 avoids overflow, and whether hi is n−1 or n decides every boundary that follows.

whatIsIt: Jump search works on a sorted array by leaping ahead in fixed-size blocks until it overshoots the target, then scanning linearly back within the last block.
It sits between linear and binary search: fewer comparisons than linear, but it only ever jumps forward, which suits data that is costly to seek backward through.

steps.title: Pick a Block Size
steps.body: Use a step of √n — the size that balances jumps against the final linear scan.

steps.title: Jump Forward
steps.body: Skip ahead one block at a time while the block's last element is below the target.

steps.title: Overshoot
steps.body: Stop at the first block whose end is ≥ the target — the value must lie inside it.

steps.title: Linear Scan the Block
steps.body: Walk that block element by element to find the target or confirm it's absent.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: About √n jumps plus a √n scan of the final block.

formulas.label: Optimal step
formulas.note: Minimizes total work; jumps and scan cost balance here.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Only index variables are used.

notationKey.meaning: number of elements
block size, chosen as √n
start of the current block and jump distance

codeBlocks.title: Jump search

applications.title: Costly Backward Seeks
applications.body: On media where jumping back is expensive (tape, some disk layouts), forward-only jumps beat binary search's back-and-forth.

applications.title: Sorted Block Storage
applications.body: Indexes stored in fixed-size blocks map naturally onto jump search's block stride.

applications.title: Middle-Ground Lookup
applications.body: When binary search is awkward but linear is too slow, √n jumping is a simple compromise.

takeaways: Jump search needs sorted input and runs in O(√n) — between linear O(n) and binary O(log n).
The optimal block size is √n, balancing the number of jumps against the final scan.
It only moves forward, an edge when backward access is expensive.
For random-access memory, binary search's O(log n) is almost always the better choice.

figure.caption: Step forward in blocks until the value overshoots, then walk back through one block. √n is the block size that balances the two halves of that cost — O(√n) is worse than binary search's O(log n), and it exists for storage where jumping *backwards* is the expensive move, so a sequential sweep with few rewinds wins.

whatIsIt: Interpolation search improves on binary search for uniformly distributed sorted data by estimating where the target likely sits instead of always probing the middle.
It's how you find a name in a phone book: for 'Aaron' you open near the front, not the center — the probe position is guided by the target's value.

steps.title: Estimate the Position
steps.body: Interpolate a probe index from the target's value relative to the range's endpoints.

steps.title: Probe
steps.body: Compare the target to the element at the estimated index.

steps.title: Narrow the Range
steps.body: If the target is larger, search above the probe; if smaller, search below.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.body: Re-estimate within the shrunken range until the target is found or the range empties.

formulas.label: Probe formula
formulas.note: Position estimated by linear interpolation on value.

formulas.label: Uniform data
formulas.note: Near-instant on evenly spaced keys.

formulas.label: Worst case
formulas.note: Skewed or clustered data degrades it to a linear scan.

notationKey.meaning: target value
current range endpoints
the interpolated probe index

codeBlocks.title: Interpolation search

applications.title: Phone Book / Dictionary Lookup
applications.body: On evenly spread keys, jumping straight to the estimated spot beats halving repeatedly.

applications.title: Uniform Numeric Indexes
applications.body: Sorted sensor readings or timestamps spaced regularly are ideal for value-guided probing.

applications.title: Large Uniform Datasets
applications.body: The O(log log n) advantage grows with size — as long as the distribution stays uniform.

takeaways: Interpolation search guesses the probe position from the target's value, not just the midpoint.
On uniformly distributed data it reaches O(log log n) — faster than binary search.
On skewed or clustered data it collapses to O(n), so distribution matters enormously.
Use it only when data is sorted and roughly uniform; otherwise binary search's O(log n) is safer.

figure.caption: Binary search always probes the middle; this one guesses *where* the value should be from how far along the range it sits — the way you open a phone book near the back for "W". On uniformly spread data that is O(log log n). On clustered data the guess is consistently wrong and it degrades to O(n), which binary search never does.

whatIsIt: Exponential search finds a target in a sorted array by first doubling an index until it passes the target, then binary-searching the bounded range that must contain it.
It shines when the array is unbounded or huge and the target is near the front — the range is found in a logarithmic number of doublings, before any binary search runs.

steps.title: Check the First Element
steps.body: If index 0 holds the target, you're done immediately.

steps.title: Double the Bound
steps.body: Try index 1, 2, 4, 8, … until that element exceeds the target or runs off the end.

steps.title: Fix the Range
steps.body: The target, if present, lies between the previous bound and the current one.

steps.title: Binary Search the Range
steps.body: Run a standard binary search over that bracketed subarray.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: i is the target's index — doublings plus a binary search over the found range.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Iterative version needs only index variables.

formulas.label: Best when
formulas.note: Or the array size is unknown/unbounded.

notationKey.meaning: index where the target lives
the doubling probe index (1, 2, 4, …)
range handed to the binary search

codeBlocks.title: Exponential search

applications.title: Unbounded / Streaming Data
applications.body: When the array length is unknown, doubling finds a valid range without needing the size up front.

applications.title: Front-Loaded Targets
applications.body: If matches usually sit near the start, it beats plain binary search by bounding the range quickly.

applications.title: Sorted Index Probing
applications.body: Used over sorted on-disk or remote indexes where reads are sequential and cheap early on.

takeaways: Exponential search doubles to bracket the target, then binary-searches that range, in O(log i).
It is ideal for unbounded arrays or when the target is near the front.
It requires sorted data, just like the binary search it delegates to.
For a bounded array with a random target position, plain binary search is simpler and equivalent.

figure.caption: For input with no known end — a stream, an unbounded array, an API that pages — double the bound until it overshoots, then binary-search the last doubling. Finding the range costs O(log i) in the *answer's* position rather than the collection's size, which is what makes it beat a plain binary search when the target sits near the front.

whatIsIt: Breadth-first search (BFS) explores a graph or tree level by level, visiting all neighbors of a node before moving to the next level.
Think of ripples spreading from a stone dropped in water — BFS visits everything at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on.

steps.title: Start at the Source
steps.body: Enqueue the starting node and mark it visited.

steps.title: Dequeue & Expand
steps.body: Remove the front of the queue and enqueue any unvisited neighbors.

steps.title: Mark as Visited
steps.body: Mark each node visited the moment it's enqueued, not when it's dequeued, to avoid duplicate visits.

steps.title: Repeat Until Empty
steps.body: Continue until the queue is empty — every reachable node has now been visited in order of distance.

formulas.label: Time complexity
formulas.note: Every vertex is dequeued once, every edge is examined once.

formulas.label: Space complexity
formulas.note: The queue and visited set can each hold up to all vertices.

formulas.label: Shortest path (unweighted)
formulas.note: BFS finds shortest paths by hop count in unweighted graphs.

notationKey.meaning: number of vertices
number of edges
set of nodes already enqueued

codeBlocks.title: Breadth-First Search

applications.title: Shortest Path (Unweighted)
applications.body: Finding the fewest number of hops/moves — puzzle solvers, social-network 'degrees of separation.'

applications.title: Web Crawling
applications.body: Crawlers visit pages level by level from a seed URL, mirroring BFS's queue-driven expansion.

applications.title: Broadcast/Flood Fill
applications.body: Flood-fill in image editors and network broadcast both spread outward exactly like BFS.

takeaways: BFS uses a queue (FIFO) — that's what forces level-by-level exploration.
In an unweighted graph, BFS is guaranteed to find the shortest path in terms of edge count.
Marking nodes visited at enqueue time, not dequeue time, is essential to avoid processing a node twice.
DFS explores deep first with a stack; BFS explores wide first with a queue — same graph, opposite traversal shape.

figure.caption: Labels are the distance from A, and BFS assigns them in the order it visits: A, B, C, D, E, F — one whole layer before the next begins. The queue is what enforces that, and it is why the label a node gets the first time it is seen is already final: on an unweighted graph nothing found later can be closer. Give the edges different weights and that stops being true, which is the entire reason Dijkstra exists. B–C connects two nodes on the same layer, so it can never be a tree edge — in an undirected BFS every non-tree edge joins nodes at most one layer apart, and that is what makes odd cycles (and bipartiteness) detectable in the same pass.

whatIsIt: Depth-first search explores a graph by going as deep as possible along one path before backtracking to try the next unexplored branch.
It uses a stack — explicit, or implicitly via recursion — so the most recently discovered node is the next one expanded.

steps.title: Visit & Mark
steps.body: Start at a source node, mark it visited so it's never processed twice.

steps.title: Go Deeper
steps.body: Recurse into the first unvisited neighbor, then its unvisited neighbor, and so on.

steps.title: Backtrack
steps.body: When a node has no unvisited neighbors, return to the previous node and try its next branch.

steps.title: Repeat Until Done
steps.body: Continue until every node reachable from the source has been visited.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: Each vertex and edge is examined once.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: Recursion/stack depth plus the visited set.

formulas.label: Traversal order
formulas.note: Explores a branch fully before its siblings.

notationKey.meaning: number of vertices (nodes)
number of edges
set marking already-explored nodes

codeBlocks.title: DFS — recursive

applications.title: Cycle & Connectivity Checks
applications.body: DFS detects cycles, finds connected components, and drives topological sort on dependency graphs.

applications.title: Maze & Puzzle Solving
applications.body: Exploring one path fully before backing up is the backbone of backtracking search.

applications.title: Path & Tree Traversal
applications.body: Pre/in/post-order tree walks and 'does a path exist?' queries are DFS in disguise.

takeaways: DFS goes deep first and backtracks, driven by a stack (often the call stack via recursion).
It runs in O(V + E) and needs a visited set to avoid revisiting nodes in cyclic graphs.
It underpins cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, and backtracking.
Use DFS when you must exhaust paths; use BFS when you need the shortest unweighted path.

figure.caption: The same graph BFS's page uses, numbered by visit order instead of by distance: A, B, C, E, F, D. The tree is one long chain, because DFS commits to a direction and only reconsiders when it runs out of room — deep and narrow where BFS is shallow and wide, on identical input. A–C is a back edge, reaching a node still open on the current path, and back edges are exactly what cycle detection watches for; the ancestor relation they expose is what Tarjan's low-links generalise. The cost is the stack: recursion depth is O(V) here rather than O(width), so a long graph overflows a DFS that a BFS would have walked fine.

whatIsIt: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from a single source to every other node in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
It is greedy: at each step it locks in the closest unfinished node, confident that no cheaper route to it can appear later — a guarantee that holds only when weights are non-negative.

steps.title: Initialize Distances
steps.body: Source distance is 0; every other node starts at infinity.

steps.title: Pick the Closest
steps.body: From a min-priority queue, take the unvisited node with the smallest known distance.

steps.title: Relax Neighbors
steps.body: For each neighbor, if going through the current node is cheaper, update its distance.

steps.title: Finalize & Repeat
steps.body: Mark the node done — its distance is now final — and repeat until all nodes are settled.

formulas.label: With a binary heap
formulas.note: Each edge may trigger a heap update.

formulas.label: Relaxation
formulas.formula: if d[u] + w < d[v]: d[v] = d[u] + w
formulas.note: Improve a neighbor's best-known distance.

formulas.label: Requires
formulas.note: Negative edges break the greedy guarantee — use Bellman-Ford instead.

notationKey.meaning: best known distance from the source to v
weight of an edge
vertices and edges

codeBlocks.title: Dijkstra with a priority queue

applications.title: GPS & Routing
applications.body: Navigation apps compute fastest routes over road networks with Dijkstra and its heuristic cousin A*.

applications.title: Network Routing
applications.body: Link-state protocols like OSPF run Dijkstra to build shortest-path routing tables.

applications.title: Game Pathfinding
applications.body: Units find least-cost paths across weighted terrain grids using Dijkstra-based search.

takeaways: Dijkstra greedily settles the nearest node first, giving single-source shortest paths.
It requires non-negative edge weights; negative edges need Bellman-Ford.
A min-priority queue brings it to O((V + E) log V).
Add a goal heuristic and it becomes A*, the standard for point-to-point pathfinding.

figure.caption: Final distances, settled in increasing order: S at 0, A at 2, B at 3, C at 5. B was labelled 5 at first, by the direct edge from S, and dropped to 3 once A was relaxed — relaxation only ever lowers a label, never raises one. The greedy step is declaring A final while B still read 5, and it is sound only because every weight is non-negative: no path leaving A can come back cheaper than the label it already has. One negative edge anywhere breaks that reasoning — a distance locked in early could be undercut later — which is the whole reason Bellman-Ford exists.

whatIsIt: Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that doesn't form a cycle, until every node is connected.
It is edge-centric and greedy: sort all edges by weight, then grow a forest of trees that gradually merge into one, using a disjoint-set structure to detect cycles.

steps.title: Sort the Edges
steps.body: Order every edge by weight, cheapest first.

steps.title: Take the Cheapest
steps.body: Consider edges in that order, one at a time.

steps.title: Reject Cycles
steps.body: Add the edge only if its endpoints are in different components; skip it otherwise.

steps.title: Stop at V − 1 Edges
steps.body: Once the tree has V − 1 edges it spans all nodes and is minimal.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: Dominated by sorting the edges.

formulas.label: Cycle check
formulas.note: Near-constant per query with path compression + union by rank.

formulas.label: Tree size
formulas.note: A spanning tree of V nodes has exactly V − 1 edges.

notationKey.meaning: vertices and edges
minimum spanning tree — connects all nodes at least total cost
disjoint-set operations detecting/merging components

codeBlocks.title: Kruskal with union-find

applications.title: Network Design
applications.body: Lay cable, pipe, or road between sites at minimum total cost while keeping everything connected.

applications.title: Clustering
applications.body: Cutting the most expensive MST edges partitions data into natural clusters.

applications.title: Circuit & Grid Layout
applications.body: Minimizing wiring length across components maps directly onto an MST.

takeaways: Kruskal adds cheapest edges globally, skipping any that would form a cycle.
Its O(E log E) cost is dominated by sorting; union-find makes cycle checks near-instant.
It naturally handles disconnected input, building a minimum spanning forest.
Prefer Kruskal for sparse, edge-listed graphs; Prim's suits dense, adjacency-based ones.

figure.caption: Edges considered cheapest-first: 1, 2, 3, then 4 — which is rejected. Not for being expensive, but because B and C already sit in the same component by then, so adding it would close a cycle; that is the only test Kruskal ever performs, and a disjoint-set structure answers it in near-constant time. Drawn here is the finished tree; mid-run it would not look like a tree at all, because after 1 and 2 there are two disconnected fragments and nothing joining them — Prim's never has that stage. The run stops at V − 1 = 4 edges, so the edge weighted 6 is never examined at all. Total weight 11, and the sort dominates: O(E log E).

whatIsIt: Prim's algorithm grows a minimum spanning tree from a single starting node, repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that connects the tree to a node not yet in it.
Where Kruskal thinks in edges, Prim is node-centric: it keeps one connected tree the whole time and extends its frontier greedily.

steps.title: Start Anywhere
steps.body: Put one arbitrary node into the tree.

steps.title: Look at the Frontier
steps.body: Consider every edge crossing from the tree to a node outside it.

steps.title: Add the Cheapest Crossing Edge
steps.body: Pick the lightest such edge and pull its outside node into the tree.

steps.title: Repeat Until Spanned
steps.body: Keep extending the frontier until all nodes are in the tree.

formulas.label: With a binary heap
formulas.note: A min-heap holds candidate crossing edges.

formulas.label: Dense graphs
formulas.note: A simple array scan can beat the heap when E ≈ V².

formulas.label: Invariant
formulas.note: The chosen edges always form a single growing tree.

notationKey.meaning: vertices and edges
cheapest edge weight connecting v to the current tree
edges crossing from tree to non-tree nodes

applications.title: Utility & Network Layout
applications.body: Connect all sites at minimum cost when the graph is dense and given as adjacency lists.

applications.title: Maze Generation
applications.body: Randomized-weight Prim's carves connected, loop-free mazes.

applications.title: Approximate TSP
applications.body: MSTs from Prim's seed 2-approximation heuristics for the traveling salesman problem.

takeaways: Prim's grows one tree outward, always adding the cheapest edge to a new node.
With a heap it runs in O((V + E) log V); a plain array is better on dense graphs at O(V²).
It and Kruskal both yield a minimum spanning tree — the choice is graph density and representation.
Its always-connected invariant makes it a natural fit for adjacency-list graphs.

figure.caption: The same graph Kruskal's page uses, caught mid-run. The tree so far is {A, B} and the only edges that exist as far as Prim is concerned are the ones crossing out of it: 3 beats 4, so C joins next. Look at the edge weighted 2 — it is the cheapest edge left anywhere in the graph and Prim will not look at it yet, because neither end is in the tree. Kruskal would already have taken it. That is the real difference: one connected tree growing across a cut, never a forest, so no cycle test is needed at all — an edge into a node already inside simply is not a crossing edge. Same MST, weight 11, different order.

whatIsIt: The fractional knapsack problem fills a weight-limited bag to maximize value, where items may be taken in any fraction — half an item is allowed.
That divisibility is what makes it greedy-solvable: always take from the item with the best value-per-weight first, unlike the all-or-nothing 0/1 knapsack which needs dynamic programming.

steps.title: Compute Value Density
steps.body: For each item calculate value ÷ weight — its worth per unit of capacity.

steps.title: Sort by Density
steps.body: Order items from highest value-per-weight to lowest.

steps.title: Take Whole Items
steps.body: Add items fully while they still fit in the remaining capacity.

steps.title: Take a Fraction
steps.body: When the next item won't fully fit, take just the fraction that fills the bag.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: Dominated by sorting items by value density.

formulas.label: Greedy key
formulas.note: Highest density first is provably optimal here.

formulas.label: Divisibility
formulas.note: Removing it turns this into NP-hard 0/1 knapsack.

notationKey.meaning: the bag's weight capacity
value and weight of item i
value ÷ weight, the greedy sort key

applications.title: Resource Allocation
applications.body: Divisible budgets — spread money across investments by best return per dollar.

applications.title: Bandwidth & Cargo
applications.body: Allocating continuous resources like bandwidth or bulk cargo to maximize value fits directly.

applications.title: Greedy Teaching Example
applications.body: It's the textbook case where a simple greedy choice is provably optimal.

takeaways: Fractional knapsack is optimally solved by greed: highest value-per-weight first.
It runs in O(n log n), all in the sort — the fill pass is linear.
Allowing fractions is essential; the 0/1 version is NP-hard and needs DP.
It is a canonical example that greed works only when the problem has the right structure.

figure.caption: Capacity 50 kg, and three items taken in value-per-kilogram order: A at 6/kg fills 10 kg, B at 5/kg fills 20, and C at 4/kg only partly fits — so two thirds of it goes in and the bag closes exactly full, for 60 + 100 + 80 = 240. The slice is the entire reason greed is exact here: the bag never ends with wasted capacity, so no other arrangement can beat filling it with the densest material available. Forbid the slice and the argument collapses immediately — that is 0/1 knapsack, and it needs a table. Everything here is one sort: O(n log n).

whatIsIt: Huffman coding compresses data by giving frequent symbols short bit codes and rare symbols long ones, minimizing the total encoded length.
It greedily builds a binary tree from the bottom up, always merging the two least-frequent symbols, so the resulting prefix-free code is provably optimal for symbol-by-symbol encoding.

steps.title: Count Frequencies
steps.body: Tally how often each symbol appears in the input.

steps.title: Merge the Two Smallest
steps.body: Repeatedly take the two lowest-frequency nodes from a min-heap and join them under a new parent.

steps.title: Build the Tree
steps.body: The merged parent's frequency is the sum; reinsert it and repeat until one root remains.

steps.title: Read Off Codes
steps.body: Label left edges 0 and right edges 1; each leaf's root-to-leaf path is its code.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: n symbols, each heap push/pop is O(log n).

formulas.label: Prefix-free
formulas.formula: no code is a prefix of another
formulas.note: Guarantees unambiguous decoding.

formulas.label: Optimality
formulas.note: Shortest possible per-symbol code.

notationKey.meaning: how often symbol i occurs
bit-length of symbol i's code
codes where none is a prefix of another

codeBlocks.title: Building the Huffman tree

applications.title: File Compression
applications.body: ZIP, gzip, and PNG use Huffman coding (often after other passes) to shrink data losslessly.

applications.title: Media Codecs
applications.body: JPEG and MP3 entropy-code their quantized coefficients with Huffman tables.

applications.title: Protocol Header Compression
applications.body: HTTP/2's HPACK uses a static Huffman code to shrink repeated header strings.

takeaways: Huffman coding assigns shorter codes to more frequent symbols, minimizing total bits.
It greedily merges the two least-frequent nodes, building an optimal prefix-free tree.
The prefix-free property is what lets a decoder split the bitstream unambiguously.
It is optimal per-symbol; adaptive and arithmetic coders can beat it by modeling context.

figure.caption: Frequencies A:5, B:2, C:1, D:1, merged two-smallest-first — so the rarest symbols are buried the deepest and end up with the longest codes, which is the entire compression argument. Depth is code length: A costs 1 bit, B 2, C and D 3 each, for 5·1 + 2·2 + 1·3 + 1·3 = 15 bits against 18 for fixed two-bit codes. Every symbol sits at a leaf and no internal node holds one, which is what makes the code prefix-free: the decoder can read bits until it falls off the tree and never needs a separator. Internal nodes carry the summed frequency and nothing else.

whatIsIt: Job sequencing with deadlines schedules unit-time jobs, each with a deadline and a profit, on a single machine to maximize total profit — every job earns its profit only if finished by its deadline.
The greedy insight: consider jobs by profit high-to-low, and place each as late as its deadline allows, keeping late slots open for the profitable jobs still to come.

steps.title: Sort by Profit
steps.body: Order jobs from highest profit to lowest.

steps.title: Find a Late Slot
steps.body: For each job, look for a free time slot at or before its deadline, latest first.

steps.title: Schedule If Possible
steps.body: Place the job in that slot; if no free slot ≤ its deadline exists, skip it.

steps.title: Sum the Profit
steps.body: Total the profits of all successfully scheduled jobs.

formulas.note: Each job scans backward for a free slot.

formulas.label: Union-find version
formulas.note: Disjoint-set finds the latest free slot near-instantly.

Placing jobs late leaves earlier slots open for other deadline-bound jobs.

It is a clean example of a greedy choice plus a smart data structure for the bottleneck.

figure.caption: Three unit-length slots, jobs placed profit-first: J1 earns 100 by deadline 2, J2 earns 60 by deadline 1, J4 earns 20 by deadline 3. J1 goes into slot 2, not slot 1 — as late as its deadline permits — and that is the whole trick. Placed early it would have occupied the only slot J2 can ever use, and 60 would have been lost for nothing. J3 (40 by deadline 2) arrives to find both slots at or before 2 already filled and is dropped: a job is skipped only when every slot it could legally use is gone. Total 180.

whatIsIt: Given a set of activities, each with a start and a finish time, activity selection asks for the largest number of them you can run on a single resource without any two overlapping. It is the interval-scheduling problem in its purest form: no weights, no priorities, just count.

The answer is one line — sort by finish time, then sweep left to right taking any activity that starts at or after the last one you took. What makes this worth studying is not the code but why the code is correct, because the three obvious alternatives are all wrong. Earliest start first fails on a single activity that opens the day and closes it. Shortest duration first fails on a short activity wedged between two long ones it blocks. Fewest conflicts first survives longer but still has counterexamples. Earliest finish first has none.

The proof is an exchange argument. Let a₁ be the activity that finishes first and let S be any optimal schedule. If S already contains a₁ there is nothing to show. If it does not, take S's own first activity and swap it for a₁: a₁ finishes no later, so it cannot conflict with anything else in S, and the swap leaves a schedule of the same size that does contain a₁. The remaining problem is the same problem on the activities that start after a₁ finishes, so induction closes it. That structure — a greedy choice that is always safe, plus a subproblem of the same shape — is exactly what the greedy method needs and what fractional knapsack has too.

steps.title: Sort by Finish Time

steps.title: Take the First

steps.title: Track the Last Finish
steps.body: Keep one variable: the finish time of the most recently selected activity.

steps.title: Sweep and Test
steps.body: For each remaining activity in finish order, take it if start ≥ last finish, otherwise skip it.

whatIsIt: Greedy coin change makes an amount out of the fewest coins by repeatedly taking the largest denomination that still fits. On the coins in your pocket it is what you already do without thinking: 68¢ becomes 25 + 25 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1, and no shorter answer exists.

But the correctness comes from the denominations, not from the algorithm. With coins {1, 3, 4} and a target of 6, greed takes 4, then can only add 1 + 1 — three coins — while 3 + 3 does it in two. Nothing about the greedy rule is at fault; the coin system simply does not have the structure that makes the rule safe. The simulation runs both the greedy sweep and the DP table on exactly this input so the failure is watched rather than asserted.

A coin system where greed is always optimal is called canonical. There is no simple arithmetic characterisation of canonical systems, but there is a decision procedure: Pearson's algorithm finds the smallest counterexample, if one exists, in O(n³) time for n denominations, by checking only a bounded set of candidate amounts derived from the greedy representations. Real currencies are canonical because they are designed to be — the 1-2-5 pattern of most banknote series is a deliberate choice, not an accident. When you cannot guarantee canonicity, the DP formulation is the correct algorithm, and it costs O(amount × n) rather than O(n log n).

steps.title: Check the System, Not the Run

whatIsIt: The factorial of n (written n!) is the product of all positive integers up to n, and it's the classic first example of recursion: n! = n × (n−1)!.
It shows the two ingredients every recursive function needs — a base case that stops the recursion (0! = 1) and a recursive case that shrinks the problem toward it.

steps.title: Base Case
steps.body: Define the stopping point: 0! = 1 (and 1! = 1). Without it the recursion never ends.

steps.title: Recursive Case
steps.body: Express the answer in terms of a smaller one: n! = n × (n−1)!.

steps.title: Wind Down
steps.body: Each call defers its multiplication and calls itself with n−1, stacking frames until the base case.

steps.title: Unwind
steps.body: Hitting the base case, the stack resolves back up, multiplying results on the way out.

steps.title: Identify Overlap
steps.body: Naive recursion recomputes F(n−2) many times — those repeated subproblems are the target.

steps.title: Memoize (Top-Down)
steps.body: Recurse as usual but store each F(n) the first time; return the cached value on repeat calls.

steps.title: Tabulate (Bottom-Up)
steps.body: Fill an array left to right: each entry is the sum of the two before it.

steps.title: Shrink the State
steps.body: Only the last two values matter, so two variables replace the whole table — O(1) space.

formulas.label: Recurrence
formulas.note: The same relation, now computed once each.

formulas.note: Each subproblem solved a single time.

takeaways: Storing subproblem results turns exponential recursion into linear DP.
Top-down memoization and bottom-up tabulation are two routes to the same answer.
When only recent states matter, roll the table into a few variables for O(1) space.
Fibonacci is the minimal example of DP's core idea: solve each subproblem once.

figure.caption: The same numbers the naive recursion recomputed exponentially, each written exactly once. There are only n distinct subproblems no matter how many times the recursion asked for them, so filling left to right is linear — and the direction is the only thing that differs from top-down memoisation, which fills the same cells in the order the calls happen to reach them. The band is the second observation: a cell reads nothing but its two predecessors, so the array can be thrown away and two variables kept instead, which is why the practical version is O(1) space.

whatIsIt: The longest common subsequence (LCS) of two strings is the longest sequence of characters appearing in both in the same order, though not necessarily contiguously.
It's a foundational two-string DP: a table indexed by prefixes of each string, where each cell extends or inherits the best subsequence found so far.

steps.title: Compare Prefixes
steps.body: dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i chars of A and first j chars of B.

steps.title: Match Extends
steps.body: If A[i] == B[j], the LCS grows by one: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1.

steps.title: Mismatch Inherits
steps.body: Otherwise take the better of dropping a character from A or from B.

steps.title: Fill & Trace
steps.body: Fill the grid row by row; walk back from the corner to reconstruct the actual subsequence.

formulas.label: Match
formulas.note: When characters agree.

formulas.label: Mismatch
formulas.note: Drop one character from either string.

formulas.label: Time / Space
formulas.note: One cell per prefix pair; space reducible to O(min(m, n)).

in-order but not necessarily contiguous characters

takeaways: LCS is the archetypal two-string DP over prefix pairs.
Matching characters extend the diagonal; mismatches inherit the best neighbor.
It runs in O(m · n), reducible to O(min(m, n)) space if only the length is needed.
Diffing, sequence alignment, and edit distance are all close relatives.

figure.caption: A = ABC down the side, B = ACB across the top, and every cell is one comparison of two prefixes. On a match the value comes from the diagonal plus one â the two characters pair off and both prefixes shrink. On a mismatch nothing is paid and nothing is added: the cell copies the better of its two neighbours, because the answer is a length being maximised rather than a cost being minimised. That is the whole difference from edit distance, which reads three neighbours and always adds one. The corner reads 2 (AB or AC), and walking back along the arrows recovers which characters those were.

whatIsIt: The 0/1 knapsack problem maximizes the value packed into a weight-limited bag where each item is taken whole or left behind — no fractions allowed.
That all-or-nothing constraint defeats greedy strategies, so it's solved by dynamic programming over a table of (items considered, capacity used).

steps.title: Define the State
steps.body: dp[i][w] = the best value using the first i items within capacity w.

steps.title: Take or Leave
steps.body: For item i, choose the better of skipping it or including it (value plus dp for the reduced capacity).

steps.title: Fill the Table
steps.body: Build up from zero items and zero capacity to the full problem.

steps.title: Read the Answer
steps.body: dp[n][W] holds the maximum achievable value; backtrack the table to recover which items.

formulas.label: Transition
formulas.note: Leave vs take item i.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: One cell per item-capacity pair — pseudo-polynomial.

formulas.label: Space
formulas.note: A single rolling row suffices if items aren't recovered.

value and weight of item i
best value from first i items in capacity w

takeaways: 0/1 knapsack is DP over (items, capacity) with a take-or-leave choice per item.
It runs in pseudo-polynomial O(n · W); iterating capacity downward keeps items single-use.
Greedy fails here — that's exactly what separates it from fractional knapsack.
Backtracking the filled table recovers which items were chosen, not just the value.

figure.caption: Three items — weight 2 value 3, weight 3 value 5, weight 4 value 6 — against a bag of capacity 6. Each row adds one item to the pool, so the take arrow always reaches into the row *above*: item 3 is used at most once, which is exactly what 0/1 means and exactly what greedy value-per-weight cannot honour. The corner is 9, from items 1 and 3 filling the bag exactly. Which items those were is not stored anywhere — it is recovered by walking back up the last column and noting every row where the value changed. The table is n·W cells, and W is a magnitude rather than an input length, so this is pseudo-polynomial: a capacity of a billion is one number to type and an impossible table to fill.

whatIsIt: Edit distance (Levenshtein distance) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or substitutions needed to turn one string into another.
Like LCS it's a two-string DP over prefixes, but each cell minimizes a cost rather than maximizing a length.

steps.title: Define the State
steps.body: dp[i][j] = the edit distance between the first i chars of A and first j chars of B.

steps.title: Match Costs Nothing
steps.body: If A[i] == B[j], carry the diagonal cost unchanged.

steps.title: Otherwise +1
steps.body: Take the cheapest of insert, delete, or substitute — each adds one to a neighbor.

steps.title: Seed the Borders
steps.body: Row 0 and column 0 are 0..n: the cost of building from an empty string.

formulas.note: Characters agree — no edit.

formulas.label: Edit
formulas.note: Delete, insert, or substitute.

formulas.label: Time / Space
formulas.note: Space reducible to O(min(m, n)) with two rows.

takeaways: Edit distance minimizes insert/delete/substitute operations via a two-string DP.
Matching characters inherit the diagonal; any edit costs one plus the best neighbor.
It runs in O(m · n), reducible to O(min(m, n)) space with rolling rows.
It's the cost-minimizing sibling of LCS and the backbone of fuzzy string matching.

figure.caption: sun → sat, and the marked cell has three ways in rather than LCS's two: the diagonal is a substitution, the cell above a deletion, the cell to the left an insertion. All three cost one, so the cell is 1 + the cheapest of them — unless the characters match, in which case the diagonal is carried through free and nothing is added at all. The borders are not zeros either: row 0 counts 0..n because turning an empty string into a prefix of length n costs n insertions. The corner is 2, which is u→a and n→t.

whatIsIt: Matrix chain multiplication finds the cheapest way to parenthesize a product of matrices — the result is identical, but the order of multiplications drastically changes the scalar-multiplication count.
It's the canonical interval DP: solve every subchain, and for each, try every split point, combining the two halves' costs plus the cost of joining them.

steps.title: Dimensions, Not Values
steps.body: Only the matrix dimensions matter; a chain A₁…Aₙ is given as a size array p where Aᵢ is p[i−1] × p[i].

steps.title: Interval State
steps.body: dp[i][j] = the minimum cost to multiply matrices i through j.

steps.title: Try Every Split
steps.body: For each split k between i and j, cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + joining cost.

steps.title: Grow by Length
steps.body: Fill intervals shortest to longest so every sub-answer is ready.

formulas.label: Join cost
formulas.note: Scalar multiplications to combine the two halves.

formulas.label: Transition
formulas.formula: dp[i][j] = min over k of (dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + join)
formulas.note: Best split point.

formulas.label: Time / Space
formulas.note: n² intervals, each trying up to n splits.

notationKey.meaning: number of matrices in the chain

takeaways: Parenthesization doesn't change the result but hugely changes the multiplication cost.

figure.caption: A₁ is 10×30, A₂ is 30×5, A₃ is 5×60 — the values never enter it, only the shapes. The cell for the whole chain tries both places the *last* multiplication could happen. Splitting after A₂ costs 1500 + 0 + 10·5·60 = 4500; splitting after A₁ costs 0 + 9000 + 10·30·60 = 27000. Same product, six times the arithmetic. whatIsIt: The longest increasing subsequence (LIS) is the longest run of strictly increasing values you can pull from a sequence while keeping their original order.
It has two classic solutions: an intuitive O(n²) DP, and a slicker O(n log n) method that keeps the smallest possible tail for each length using binary search.

steps.title: DP State
steps.body: dp[i] = the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending exactly at index i.

steps.title: Extend from the Left
steps.body: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over all earlier j with a[j] < a[i].

steps.title: The n log n Trick
steps.body: Maintain 'tails': tails[k] is the smallest possible ending value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.

steps.title: Binary Search Insert
steps.body: For each value, replace the first tail ≥ it (or append) — the tails array's length is the LIS length.

formulas.label: DP transition
formulas.formula: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] : j < i, a[j] < a[i])
formulas.note: Straightforward O(n²).

formulas.label: Patience method
formulas.note: Binary-search each element into the tails array.

formulas.label: Answer
formulas.note: The longest achievable increasing run.

notationKey.meaning: length of the sequence
LIS length ending at index i
smallest tail of any length-(k+1) increasing subsequence

takeaways: LIS keeps the longest strictly increasing subsequence in original order.
The simple DP is O(n²); the patience/binary-search method is O(n log n).
The tails array trick stores the best (smallest) ending value per subsequence length.

figure.caption: The aux row is dp[i]: the longest increasing run ending *exactly* at i. Computing one cell means scanning every earlier cell with a smaller value, which is where the O(n²) comes from, and the answer is the maximum anywhere in that row rather than its last entry — the 4 at index 5 happens to be last here, but the 9 could have been a 0 and the answer would still be 4. The subsequence itself is 1, 4, 5, 9, and it is not contiguous. The O(n log n) version drops dp entirely and keeps a tails array instead — tails[k] is the smallest value any length-k+1 run can end on — binary-searching each value into place. Its length is the answer, but its contents are not a real subsequence.

whatIsIt: Coin change asks for the fewest coins (or the number of distinct ways) to make a target amount from a set of denominations.

steps.title: Base Case
steps.body: dp[0] = 0 — zero coins make amount zero.

steps.title: Try Each Coin
steps.body: For every amount, dp[a] = 1 + min over coins c of dp[a − c].

steps.title: Build Upward
steps.body: Fill dp from 1 to target so every smaller subproblem is ready when needed.

formulas.formula: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a − c]) over coins c

whatIsIt: Rod cutting maximizes revenue from a rod of length n, given a price for each possible piece length — you decide where, if at all, to cut it.
It's a clean unbounded-DP example: each length can be used any number of times, and the best value for length n is built from the best values for shorter lengths.

steps.title: State by Length
steps.body: dp[len] = the maximum revenue obtainable from a rod of length len.

steps.title: Try Every First Cut
steps.body: For length len, try each first piece i and add its price to dp[len − i].

steps.title: Keep the Best
steps.body: dp[len] is the maximum over all those first-cut choices.

steps.title: Build Upward
steps.body: Compute dp from 1 to n so each subproblem is solved before it's used.

formulas.formula: dp[len] = max over i of (price[i] + dp[len − i])
formulas.note: Cut off a piece of length i, solve the rest.

whatIsIt: Bitmask DP encodes a set as the bits of an integer, so "which items have I used so far" becomes an array index instead of a collection.

That turns an exponential search over subsets into a table of 2^n entries filled once. The canonical example is the travelling salesman problem: dp[mask][i] is the cheapest way to visit exactly the cities in `mask` and stop at city i — O(2^n · n²) instead of O(n!).

steps.title: Number the Items
steps.body: Item k owns bit k, so a subset is one integer in [0, 2^n).

steps.title: Define dp[mask][last]
steps.body: Best cost to have covered exactly `mask`, currently sitting at `last`.

steps.title: Iterate Masks Upward
steps.body: Masks only ever grow, so processing them in increasing numeric order respects the dependency order.

steps.title: Extend by One Bit
steps.body: From (mask, last), move to an unused city next: dp[mask | 1<<next][next] = min(…, dp[mask][last] + cost).

steps.title: Close the Tour
steps.body: Answer = min over last of dp[full][last] + cost(last → start).

formulas.label: TSP transition
formulas.formula: dp[mask | 1<<j][j] = min(dp[mask][i] + c[i][j])  for j ∉ mask
formulas.note: One city added per step.

formulas.label: Subset count
formulas.note: Practical only up to n ≈ 20–22.

formulas.label: Time / space
formulas.note: Every (mask, last, next) triple is examined once.

// Every subset of `mask`, largest first, in O(2^|mask|).

whatIsIt: Tree DP is dynamic programming where the subproblems are subtrees: each node's answer is assembled from its children's answers during a post-order traversal.

Because a tree has no cycles, every subtree is solved exactly once and the whole DP costs O(n). The recurring pattern is a small state per node — most often "best answer if this node is used" versus "best if it is not".

steps.title: Root the Tree
steps.body: Pick any root; parent/child direction is what turns the graph into subproblems.

steps.title: Define the State
steps.body: dp[v][s] = the answer for v's subtree given that v is in state s (taken / not taken, coloured, matched…).

steps.title: Recurse Post-Order
steps.body: Solve every child before the parent — the parent's transition reads only finished values.

steps.title: Combine the Children
steps.body: Sum or max over children according to what the parent's state permits.

steps.title: Read the Root
steps.body: The overall answer is the best state at the root — or, for path problems, a maximum tracked during the merge.

formulas.label: Max independent set
formulas.note: Taking v forbids taking any child.

formulas.label: Subtree size
formulas.note: The simplest tree DP there is.

formulas.label: Tree diameter
formulas.formula: answer = max over v of (h₁ + h₂)
formulas.note: The two deepest child heights meeting at v.

formulas.label: Time
formulas.note: Each edge contributes to exactly one merge.

notationKey.meaning: best value for the subtree rooted at v with v in state s
a child of v
children finished before the parent is computed
